records.title: Proxy Location rewrite: a same-origin absolute or network-path Location under the base path becomes an origin-less path with the client-side prefix, unless rewriteLocation(false)

metadata.Tags: 0.12.0, feasibility:high, request-b, proxy, response, location, security

acceptanceCriteria.text: On `app.use("/api/orders", Proxy.to("http://127.0.0.1:<port>"))` a backend `Location: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/orders/x` reaches the client as `Location: /api/orders/x`, while with `.rewriteLocation(false)` the client receives the original value, and the package-private accessor reports `rewriteLocation` `true` on `Proxy.to(url)`.
A relative `Location` (`/x` and `x/y`), a URL of another host (`http://other.example/x`) and, for the target `http://h:808`, the URL `http://h:8080/x` each reach the client unchanged.
With `.stripPrefix(true)` on a mount at `/api/orders`, a backend `Location: http://<target host:port>/x` reaches the client as `Location: /api/orders/x`.

For the target `http://h/base` on a mount at `/api/orders`, `Location: http://h/base/api/orders/y` becomes `/api/orders/y`, while `http://h/basement/y` and `http://h/other/y` reach the client unchanged.

For the target `http://h`, `Location: http://H:80/x` and `Location: HTTP://h/x` both become `/x`; for the target `https://h`, `Location: https://h:443/x` becomes `/x`; and for the target `http://h`, `Location: https://h/x` reaches the client unchanged.
A rewrite whose resulting path is empty yields `/`: for the target `http://h/base`, `Location: http://h/base` becomes `/`, and for the target `http://h`, `Location: http://h` becomes `/`.

Under `.stripPrefix(true)` the client-side prefix is the request's matched prefix `req.baseUrl()`, not the string given to `use`: a proxy mounted with `router.use("/orders", proxy)` on a router mounted with `app.use("/api", router)` turns `Location: http://<target host:port>/x` into `/api/orders/x`.
When the client sends `Host: gw.example` and `X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example`, a rewritten `Location` holds neither `gw.example` nor `evil.example` nor any other origin.
A network-path `Location: //<target host:port>/api/orders/x` is resolved against the target scheme and becomes `/api/orders/x`, while `Location: //other.example/x` reaches the client unchanged.
The part after the base path is kept unchanged: `Location: http://<target host:port>/api/orders/x?a=1#f` becomes `/api/orders/x?a=1#f`.

A rewritten value that a client would read as a network-path reference (it would start with two `/` or `\` characters, tab, CR and LF ignored) gets a leading `/.`: for the target `http://h`, `Location: http://h//evil.example/x` becomes `/.//evil.example/x`; user information is dropped and an empty port is read as omitted before the origin comparison, and a value whose host or port the `Proxy.to` grammar refuses is left unchanged.

records.title: Proxy response body relay: the backend body goes to res.relay with its Content-Length or -1, and HEAD, 204 and 304 responses relay no body after their framing headers are checked

metadata.Tags: 0.12.0, feasibility:high, request-b, proxy, response, body, relay

acceptanceCriteria.text: A backend response with `Content-Length: 10` and 10 body bytes reaches the client with `Content-Length: 10` and the same 10 bytes, and the proxy calls `res.relay` with the length 10, as a unit test with a recording `Response` shows.
A `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` backend response reaches the client with exactly the decoded body bytes, and the proxy calls `res.relay` with the length `-1`.

A backend response with neither `Content-Length` nor `Transfer-Encoding` that writes a body and then closes the connection reaches the client with every body byte, and the proxy calls `res.relay` with the length `-1`.

For a HEAD request whose backend answers `Content-Length: 1234` without a body and keeps the connection open, the client receives `Content-Length: 1234` and no body well before the read timeout, because the proxy reads no body bytes.

A backend 204 kept open after its header block reaches the client as 204 with neither body nor `Content-Length`; a backend 304 with `Content-Length: 10` makes the proxy call `res.relay` with `10` and reaches the client as 304 with no body (with `Content-Length: 10` where the adapter writes it for a 304, as the in-memory test adapter does); and a backend 304 without length headers reaches the client without `Content-Length`; in each case the proxy calls `res.relay` with `-1`, `10` and `-1` respectively and reads no body.

Whatever framing headers a response to a HEAD request, a 204 or a 304 carries, the proxy reads no body bytes and reports no `INVALID_RESPONSE` for those headers: a HEAD response and a 304 carrying `Content-Length: 10` together with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, the line `Content-Length: 10` twice, or the two lines `Content-Length: 10` and `Content-Length: 010` make the proxy call `res.relay` with `10`; a HEAD response and a 304 carrying `Content-Length: abc`, `Content-Length: -1`, `Content-Length: 99999999999999999999` (beyond `Long.MAX_VALUE`) or the two lines `Content-Length: 10` and `Content-Length: 11` make it call `res.relay` with `-1` and reach the client with their status, no body and no `Content-Length`; and a 204 carrying any of these headers reaches the client as 204 with no body, the proxy calling `res.relay` with `-1`.

records.rationale:
AC-1 ← PRD-89, PRD-150, PRD-157, PRD-207; AC-2 ← PRD-150, PRD-156; AC-3 ← PRD-150, PRD-158; AC-4 ← PRD-155, PRD-208; AC-5 ← PRD-155; fills: PRD-155 / hole / for AC-5, the request does not say which length a bodyless response passes to `relay` (design D-058); AC-6 ← PRD-155; fills: PRD-155 / hole / for AC-6, which length relay keeps when the bodyless response carries an unusable Content-Length. The order follows RFC 9112 §6.3 as the request's response table does (§3.9: the row "HEAD 요청에 대한 응답, 204, 304 — 본문을 읽지 않음" comes before the rows that make `Transfer-Encoding` with `Content-Length` and a malformed `Content-Length` an `INVALID_RESPONSE`): a HEAD response, 204 and 304 never carry a body whatever their length headers say, then `Transfer-Encoding`, then `Content-Length`, then read-until-close; PRD-155 records that these responses end without a body regardless of their length headers, so their framing headers can never make them malformed. Passing the length through `relay` keeps the backend's `Content-Length` for the client, which Express users get from `http-proxy-middleware` piping the backend response.
- [2026-11-14] AC-5 ← PRD-271. The client sees a relayed 304 Content-Length only where the adapter writes it (PRD U-2).
records.implementationNotes: - Call `res.relay` only after the header copy, the `Location` rewrite and the fixed response headers are applied (FR-PROXY-011); `relay` copies the body after the middleware returns and closes the stream whatever the outcome (FR-HTTP-037), which is where the proxy releases the backend connection. For HEAD and 304, `relay` keeps a non-negative length as `Content-Length` and sends no body; for 204 it sends neither (FR-HTTP-037). The framing decision belongs to the response parser (SEC-PROXY-004), which must decide "HEAD response, 204 or 304: no body" before it applies the `Transfer-Encoding`/`Content-Length` checks; those checks (SEC-PROXY-004 AC-4) apply only to responses that can carry a body. For a bodyless response, read `Content-Length` with the shared list parser of SEC-PROXY-003 instead of failing: when every element is digits that fit in a `long` and all elements are numerically equal (so `10` and `010` give 10), that value is the length; any other input (a non-digit element, a value beyond `Long.MAX_VALUE`, differing values) gives `-1`, and `Transfer-Encoding` is ignored. Precedence: the request's response table (§3.9, PRD-155) puts the bodyless row before the malformed-framing rows, so it overrides run design item D-058, which had the framing headers of these responses validated before the body is skipped; only D-058's choice of the length passed to `relay` (AC-5) is kept.

records.title: Proxy failures before the response: backend-side errors go to the app's error flow as ProxyException with kind and cause, without leaking the target, and an early backend response is relayed on a best-effort basis

acceptanceCriteria.text: When no backend listens on the target port, the client receives 502 and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` whose `kind()` is `CONNECT_FAILED` and whose `getCause()` is a `java.net.ConnectException`.

For a target whose host name does not resolve (for example `http://backend.invalid:8081`), the client receives 502 and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `CONNECT_FAILED` whose `getCause()` is a `java.net.UnknownHostException`.

An app whose `onError` answers a `ProxyException` with `res.status(e.status())` and a JSON body naming `kind()` makes the client receive 502 with that JSON body when the backend is down, and the proxy writes no response body of its own.

On an app without `onError`, a request to a stopped backend gets the default error response with status 502 and the standard reason phrase, and the response body contains neither the target host nor the target port.

The proxy calls the app logger for none of the failures of AC-1, AC-2 and AC-7, as a unit test that calls the middleware directly with a recording logger shows; logging them is left to the error flow.

When the backend reads part of a 1 MiB request body, sends a complete `401` response, closes only its writing direction (FIN) and reads and discards the rest of the body, the client receives that 401.

When the backend reads part of a large request body and then closes the connection without sending any response, the client receives 502 and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `INVALID_RESPONSE`.

Once a write of the request body to the backend has failed, the proxy reads no further bytes of the client body, as a unit test with a counting body stream shows, and leaves the rest of the client connection to the adapter.

When the write-timeout or total-timeout watchdog closes the backend socket while the request body is being written, the early-response rule does not apply: with `.writeTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).bodyLimit(128 << 20)` a 64 MiB body sent to a backend that never reads the request body gives 504 and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `WRITE_TIMEOUT`, and with `.totalTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).bodyLimit(128 << 20)` the same request gives 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT`; in neither case is the kind `INVALID_RESPONSE`.

records.requirement: The system shall make the proxy throw every backend-side failure that happens before the response is handed to `res.relay` into the app's error flow as a `ProxyException` holding the failure's kind and the underlying exception as its cause — `CONNECT_FAILED` when the connection cannot be established for a reason other than a timeout (refused, unresolvable host, TLS failure other than a timeout) and `INVALID_RESPONSE` when the response is malformed or the connection ends before a complete header block — writing neither an error body nor an app-logger entry of its own; and shall deliver an early backend response on a best-effort basis: when writing the request body fails because the backend closed or reset the connection, it tries to read the response left on the socket, relays it when a complete status line and header block arrive, reports `INVALID_RESPONSE` otherwise, and in both cases stops the body transfer and reads no more of the client body. A write failure caused by the write-timeout or total-timeout watchdog closing the socket is not such a case: it is reported with the deadline the watchdog recorded, `WRITE_TIMEOUT` or `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` (FR-PROXY-017), and never as `INVALID_RESPONSE`.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-13, PRD-97, PRD-98, PRD-211; AC-2 ← PRD-97, PRD-98; AC-3 ← PRD-9, PRD-97, PRD-230; AC-4 ← PRD-13, PRD-99, PRD-211; AC-5 ← PRD-230; fills: PRD-106 / hole / for AC-5, the request has the proxy log only failures after the response started and does not say who logs earlier ones, so they are left to the error flow and its logging (design D-062); AC-6 ← PRD-103, PRD-207; AC-7 ← PRD-103; AC-8 ← PRD-104; AC-9 ← PRD-103, PRD-109, PRD-111, PRD-211. Handing failures to the error flow (decision 5) keeps proxy errors consistent with NaruServe's default error handling and lets `onError` answer by kind, as Express users do in `http-proxy-middleware`'s `on.error` handler; a hand-made proxy that let a connect failure surface as 500 is one of the pitfalls the official proxy removes. A blocking client does not read while it writes the body, so a backend that answers 401 or 413 early and closes is caught only when the write fails; an RST discards the receive buffer, so that case stays untested best effort. The request (§3.4) scopes the early-response rule to a backend that sends a response and closes the connection, while its error table gives a write timeout 504 `WRITE_TIMEOUT` and an exceeded total limit 504 `TOTAL_TIMEOUT`; both deadlines are enforced by the watchdog closing the socket, so AC-9 keeps those write failures out of the `INVALID_RESPONSE` fallback.
records.implementationNotes: - Throw the `ProxyException` from `Middleware.handle`; never call `res.abort` and never write a body yourself. Build it with `new ProxyException(kind, cause)` (IR-PROXY-002), so the message stays `null` and the target address appears only in the cause. The slot and the watchdog are released before the exception leaves the middleware (slot and watchdog lifetime requirement). Malformed responses are defined by the response parser (SEC-PROXY-004) and TLS failures by SEC-PROXY-005; the proxy's own 400, 405 and 501 answers stay plain `HttpException` (FR-PROXY-010).

records.title: Proxy failures after the response started: the relayed stream throws an IOException caused by a ProxyException, logged to the app logger first, and the framework aborts the client connection

metadata.Tags: 0.12.0, feasibility:high, request-b, proxy, errors, abort, logging

acceptanceCriteria.text: When the backend sends `Content-Length: 100`, then 50 body bytes, and closes the connection, the client connection is closed before 100 body bytes arrive, and the app logger receives a `ProxyException` whose `kind()` is `INVALID_RESPONSE`.

When a chunked backend body breaks mid-stream with a chunk-size line longer than 4 KiB, or with a trailer section larger than 64 KiB, the client connection is aborted before the chunked body completes, and the app logger receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `INVALID_RESPONSE`.

With `.readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a backend that sends its header block and part of the body and then stops sending makes the client connection abort after about 1 second, and the app logger receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `READ_TIMEOUT`.

The `IOException` thrown by `read` of the stream the proxy passed to `res.relay` has as its `getCause()` a `ProxyException` of the failure's kind, and the proxy never calls `res.abort`, as a unit test with a recording `Response` shows.

The proxy logs each such failure exactly once, through `Logger.error(String, Throwable)` with the `ProxyException` as the throwable, and the log call happens before the `IOException` leaves the relayed stream, as a unit test with a recording logger shows.

records.requirement: The system shall make the proxy handle a backend-side failure that happens after the response was handed to `res.relay` — the connection ending before the declared length, a malformed chunk, a read timeout between body bytes or the total timeout — by logging a `ProxyException` of the failure's kind to `req.application().logger()` once and then throwing, from the relayed stream, an `IOException` whose cause is that `ProxyException`, so that the framework aborts the client connection, without the proxy calling `res.abort` itself.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-105, PRD-106, PRD-221; AC-2 ← PRD-105, PRD-106, PRD-221; AC-3 ← PRD-105, PRD-110; AC-4 ← PRD-105; AC-5 ← PRD-106 (design D-062). Once the body is copied by the framework after the middleware returned, the proxy can no longer throw into the error flow and the status line is already sent, so the only correct signal is aborting the client connection; the framework's `abort(Throwable)` does not keep its cause, so the proxy writes the kind to the app logger before throwing. Express users see the same outcome as a destroyed client socket after `http-proxy-middleware` emits `error` mid-stream.
records.implementationNotes: - Wrap the backend body stream in a package-private stream that maps every read failure to its kind (a watchdog close is mapped to the kind the watchdog recorded before closing), logs it once, and throws `new IOException(proxyException)`; the framework closes this stream after any copy outcome (FR-HTTP-037), which releases the slot. The log message may name the target; it never reaches the client.

records.title: Proxy timeouts: connect 10 s, write 60 s, read 60 s and total 5 min by default, each finite and set per Proxy, the first one reached applies, 504 before the response and an aborted client connection after it

acceptanceCriteria.text: A unit test of the proxy module reads, without waiting, the configured values of `Proxy.to(url)` through the package-private accessors: connect 10 seconds, write 60 seconds, read 60 seconds and total 5 minutes.

The proxy passes the connect timeout in milliseconds to `Socket.connect(address, timeout)` for `http` and `https` targets, and a `SocketTimeoutException` from that call becomes 504 with `kind()` `CONNECT_TIMEOUT`, as a unit test with a socket that records the call and throws shows.

With `.connectTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, an https backend that accepts the TCP connection and never answers the TLS handshake gives 504 after about 1 second, and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `CONNECT_TIMEOUT`.
With `.readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a backend that reads the request and never answers gives 504 after about 1 second, and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `READ_TIMEOUT`.

With `.writeTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).bodyLimit(128 << 20)`, sending a 64 MiB body to a backend that never reads the request body gives 504 with `kind()` `WRITE_TIMEOUT` about 1 second after the socket buffers fill.

With `.writeTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a client that sends its body in pieces separated by pauses longer than 1 second to a backend that keeps reading gets the backend's response and no `WRITE_TIMEOUT`, because time spent waiting for client body bytes is not counted.

With `.readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).totalTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a backend that trickles one byte of its header block every 500 milliseconds gives 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` after about 2 seconds, and a backend that sends its header block and then one body byte every 500 milliseconds makes the client connection abort after about 2 seconds while the app logger receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT`.

With `.readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS).totalTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a backend that never answers gives 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` after about 1 second, because the first timeout reached applies.

Timeouts are set per mount: on one backend that answers after 3 seconds, a mount with `.readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` gives 504 while a mount with `.readTimeout(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)` relays the response, and the accessor of the latter reports 300000 milliseconds.
Timing tests use configured values of a few seconds at most, while the default values are checked only through the accessors of AC-1.

The response counts as handed to `res.relay` only after the proxy's final deadline check, which runs after the backend head is read and the response headers are computed but before the response status and headers are set: a total or write deadline that fires before that check gives 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` or `WRITE_TIMEOUT` carrying none of the backend's headers, and one that fires after it takes the abort-and-log path of FR-PROXY-016.

With `.totalTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, a client that keeps trickling its request body past the deadline ends the request at the first client body read after the deadline with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT`.

records.requirement: The system shall bound every proxied exchange with four finite timeouts set per `Proxy`: `connectTimeout` (default 10 seconds) for the TCP connect and, separately, the TLS handshake; `writeTimeout` (default 60 seconds) for a backend socket write that makes no progress, not counting time spent waiting for client body bytes; `readTimeout` (default 60 seconds) from the request being sent to the first response byte and between response bytes; and `totalTimeout` (default 5 minutes) from the first attempt to the end of the request, including retries and retry waits; whichever is reached first applies, and the proxy reports `CONNECT_TIMEOUT`, `WRITE_TIMEOUT`, `READ_TIMEOUT` or `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` as 504 before the response was handed to `res.relay` and aborts the client connection after it.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-13, PRD-107, PRD-108, PRD-109, PRD-110, PRD-111, PRD-211, PRD-238 (design D-071); AC-2 ← PRD-108; AC-3 ← PRD-108, PRD-211; fills: PRD-160 / hole / for AC-3, the TCP connect and the TLS handshake are bounded separately by the connect timeout (design D-063); AC-4 ← PRD-110, PRD-211; AC-5 ← PRD-109, PRD-211; AC-6 ← PRD-109, PRD-211; AC-7 ← PRD-111, PRD-212, PRD-245; AC-8 ← PRD-112; AC-9 ← PRD-8, PRD-110; AC-10 ← PRD-211 (design D-071). No timeout defaults to unlimited, because a proxy without one holds a worker thread for as long as a backend stalls, one of the pitfalls a hand-made proxy had. A read timeout measures gaps between bytes, so it alone never bounds a request; the total timeout does, which also cuts downloads longer than 5 minutes unless the mount raises it. The option is named `totalTimeout` and the kind `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` because Node's `http-proxy` `timeout` means the incoming socket timeout (decision 14); Express users map `proxyTimeout` of `http-proxy-middleware` to `readTimeout`.
records.implementationNotes: - Blocking sockets apply `SO_TIMEOUT` to reads only, so the read timeout uses `SO_TIMEOUT` while the write timeout and the total timeout are enforced by the watchdog closing the plain socket (watchdog requirements); arm the write deadline only around each backend socket write and disarm it while the copy loop waits on the client body stream. Before closing, the watchdog records which deadline fired so the failing call maps to `WRITE_TIMEOUT` or `TOTAL_TIMEOUT`. Time values are converted as FR-PROXY-002 AC-8 states (design D-047). The total timeout cannot unblock name resolution before the socket exists nor client-side I/O, which the proxy documentation states.

records.title: Proxy retries: off by default; with retries(n) connect failures retry for every method and 502 or 503 only for bodyless safe methods unless retryUnsafeMethods(true), with retryDelay waits inside the total timeout

acceptanceCriteria.text: `Proxy.to(url)` reports through the package-private accessors 0 retries, a 200-millisecond retry delay and `retryUnsafeMethods` `false`, a bodyless `GET` through it to a backend that always answers 503 arrives exactly once, and `Proxy.to(url).retries(2).retries(0)` also delivers it exactly once.

With `.retries(2)` and a backend that always answers 503, a bodyless `GET` and a `GET` with `Content-Length: 0` each arrive at the backend exactly 3 times and the client receives the third 503 response unchanged, while a bodyless `POST` and a `GET` with a body each arrive exactly once.
With `.retries(2)` and a backend that always answers 502, a bodyless `HEAD` and a bodyless `OPTIONS` each arrive exactly 3 times.

With `.retries(2)`, a `GET` arrives exactly once when the backend answers 504, when the backend never answers and the read timeout passes, and when the backend sends a malformed response (`INVALID_RESPONSE`).
With `.retries(2)` and no backend listening, a `POST` with a body is attempted with exactly 3 connection attempts and the client receives 502 with `kind()` `CONNECT_FAILED`.

A unit test of the retry decision classifies a connect failure caused by `java.net.ConnectException`, `java.net.UnknownHostException` or `java.net.NoRouteToHostException` as retryable and one caused by a connect `SocketTimeoutException` or a `javax.net.ssl.SSLException` as not retryable.

With `.retries(2).connectTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` and an https backend that accepts TCP and never answers the TLS handshake, the backend sees exactly one TCP connection and the client receives 504 with `kind()` `CONNECT_TIMEOUT`.
With `.retryUnsafeMethods(true).retries(1)` and a backend that always answers 503, a bodyless `DELETE` arrives exactly twice and a `DELETE` with a body arrives exactly once.

Between two arrivals of the same retried request the backend observes at least 200 milliseconds when `.retryDelay` is not set, and at least 300 milliseconds with `.retryDelay(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)`.

With `.retries(5).retryDelay(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).totalTimeout(2500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)` and a backend that keeps refusing connections, exactly 3 connection attempts are made and the client receives 502 with `kind()` `CONNECT_FAILED` right after the third failure, about 2 seconds after the request started, without waiting for a fourth attempt.
With `Proxy p = Proxy.to(url).retries(2)` mounted on `/a` and `p.retries(0)` mounted on `/b`, a bodyless `GET` to a backend that always answers 503 arrives 3 times through `/a` and once through `/b`.

records.requirement: The system shall make the proxy try each request once by default and, with `.retries(n)`, up to `n` more times on a new connection each: after a TCP-level connect failure that is neither a connect timeout nor a TLS failure, for every method; after a backend 502 or 503, only when the body sent to the backend was zero bytes and the method is `GET`, `HEAD` or `OPTIONS`, or any method under `.retryUnsafeMethods(true)`; and never after a connect timeout, a TLS failure, a write, read or total timeout, an `INVALID_RESPONSE` or any other status; waiting `.retryDelay` (default 200 milliseconds) before each retry, returning the last failure without waiting when the wait would end past the total-timeout deadline, and relaying the last backend response unchanged when 502 or 503 remains after the last retry.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-114, PRD-227; AC-2 ← PRD-9, PRD-213, PRD-227; AC-3 ← PRD-227; AC-4 ← PRD-116, PRD-214; AC-5 ← PRD-9, PRD-214, PRD-227; AC-6 ← PRD-227, PRD-228; fills: PRD-227 / hole / for AC-6, the retry table names connection refused and name resolution failure as examples of one class, so every TCP-level connect failure other than a connect timeout or a TLS failure is retried (design D-064); AC-7 ← PRD-115, PRD-228; AC-8 ← PRD-215; AC-9 ← PRD-215; AC-10 ← PRD-111, PRD-212; AC-11 ← PRD-12. Retrying is off by default so no request is processed twice unasked. A connect failure happens before any request byte is sent, so the backend cannot have processed it; a backend 502 or 503 can follow processing, so only bodyless safe methods retry, and a streamed body cannot be resent. TLS failures repeat identically, a connect timeout retried would hold the worker thread for another full timeout (decision 3), and failures after the request was sent leave the processing state unknown. Express users enable the same behaviour by hand around `http-proxy-middleware`, which has no built-in retry.
records.implementationNotes: - Decide eligibility for a 502 or 503 retry from the body bytes actually written to the backend (FR-PROXY-007), so a request whose one-byte pre-read found no body counts as bodyless; keep that pre-read byte for the next attempt after a connect failure, which happens before any body byte is sent. Read and discard the header block of a retried 502 or 503 and close its connection before waiting. Each attempt opens its own connection (the backend client connection requirement), and the watchdog started before the first attempt keeps running through the waits.

records.title: Proxy concurrency limit: maxConcurrent(n) creates a counter shared by the objects derived from it, a request over the limit gets 503 CONCURRENCY_LIMIT at once without a backend connection, and there is no limit by default

acceptanceCriteria.text: On a mount with `.maxConcurrent(2)` and a backend that delays its response, of three simultaneous requests the third gets 503 at once without a backend connection, and `onError` receives a `ProxyException` with `kind()` `CONCURRENCY_LIMIT`.

On the same mount, a third request that arrives while the first two are still relaying their response bodies also gets 503, and once both bodies have been fully relayed the next request reaches the backend.
With `Proxy p = Proxy.to(url).maxConcurrent(2)` mounted on `/a` and `p.retries(0)` mounted on `/b`, three simultaneous delayed requests split across `/a` and `/b` give the same result as AC-1.

Two objects created separately as `Proxy.to(url).maxConcurrent(2)` for the same target and mounted on `/a` and `/b` do not share a counter: two simultaneous delayed requests on each path all four reach the backend.

With `Proxy p = Proxy.to(url).maxConcurrent(2)` mounted on `/a` and `p.maxConcurrent(2)` mounted on `/b`, two simultaneous delayed requests on each path all four reach the backend, because calling `maxConcurrent` again creates a new counter.

With `Proxy.to(url).maxConcurrent(2)` mounted on `/a` and an unlimited `Proxy.to(url)` mounted on `/b`, while five delayed requests through `/b` are in flight, two requests through `/a` both reach the backend.
`Proxy.to(url)` reports no limit through its package-private accessor, and twenty simultaneous requests through it to a backend that delays its response all reach the backend.

When one object created with `.maxConcurrent(1)` is mounted in two apps and a delayed request through the first app is in flight, a request through the second app gets 503 with `kind()` `CONCURRENCY_LIMIT`.

The package-private counter accessor returns the same `AtomicInteger` instance for `p` and `p.retries(0)` and a different instance for `p.maxConcurrent(2)`, and the slot is taken and returned without a lock.

records.requirement: The system shall make `.maxConcurrent(n)` give its result a new counter with the limit `n`, shared by reference by every `Proxy` later derived from that result through another option method, and a new counter again whenever `.maxConcurrent` is called on a derived object; count against the counter every in-flight request of every mount of those objects, in any app, from the moment its slot is taken to the end of the request; answer a request that finds the counter at its limit at once with 503 and `kind()` `CONCURRENCY_LIMIT`, without waiting and without connecting to the backend; and count no request of a `Proxy` that has no limit, which is the default.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-218, PRD-249; AC-2 ← PRD-218; AC-3 ← PRD-124, PRD-176, PRD-218; AC-4 ← PRD-123, PRD-125, PRD-218; AC-5 ← PRD-125; AC-6 ← PRD-218, PRD-249; AC-7 ← PRD-218, PRD-237, PRD-249 (design D-065); AC-8 ← PRD-126; AC-9 ← PRD-123, PRD-124, PRD-176. Only mounts that declare a limit are counted, so an unlimited mount to the same origin never blocks a limited one, and keeping the counter on the object needs no app-level storage or lock (decision 16). The default stays unlimited although `object.md` §14.2 bans unbounded resource defaults (design D-065): a fixed default such as 16 would answer 503 under load while worker threads are still free, surprising users only in production; deriving it from `maxWorkers` would need a public way for middleware to read `ServerOptions`, which would widen request A; without a limit the proxy follows the worker-thread budget `maxWorkers` (default 64) like any synchronous handler, and the total timeout bounds how long one request holds a thread, so no resource is unbounded and the proxy documentation states this. Waiting for a slot would itself hold a worker thread, so the answer is immediate. Express has no built-in counterpart; nginx users know the idea as `max_conns`.
records.implementationNotes: - Take a slot with a compare-and-set loop on the shared `AtomicInteger` that refuses at the limit, never with a blocking wait; derived objects copy the counter reference and the limit, while `maxConcurrent` installs a fresh counter. The slot is taken only after every check and `req.bodyStream(...)` (FR-PROXY-010) and released exactly once at the end of the request (slot and watchdog lifetime requirement).

records.title: Proxy backend HTTP/1.1 client: its own client over java.net.Socket, a new connection for every attempt with Connection: close, no reuse, and no wait on a backend that keeps the connection open

acceptanceCriteria.text: Two sequential requests through one mount reach the backend over two separate TCP connections, and a request retried twice under `.retries(2)` reaches it over three separate connections.

Every backend request carries exactly one `Connection: close` line, and when the backend answers with `Connection: keep-alive` and a complete `Content-Length` body the proxy still closes that connection after the response and sends the next request over a new connection.

The main class files of `NaruServe-proxy` reference neither `java/net/HttpURLConnection` nor any class under `java/net/http/`, as a class-reference test shows, and backend connections are made through `java.net.Socket`.

When the backend sends a complete `Content-Length` response and then keeps the connection open without closing it, the client receives the complete response without waiting for the backend to close, and on a `.maxConcurrent(1)` mount the next request reaches the backend.

records.requirement: The system shall make the proxy talk to the backend through its own minimal HTTP/1.1 client over `java.net.Socket`, without `HttpURLConnection` or `java.net.http`, opening a new connection for every attempt, sending `Connection: close` on every request, never reusing a connection, and closing the connection at the end of the request; after the response has been read to its end it may wait briefly for the backend to close first, but a backend that keeps the connection open never delays the client's response or the release of the slot.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-166, PRD-235; AC-2 ← PRD-149, PRD-166; AC-3 ← PRD-146, PRD-232; AC-4 ← PRD-167. `java.net.http.HttpClient` exists only on Java 11 and not on Android, and `HttpURLConnection` refuses `PATCH` and extension methods on the JDK, blocks restricted headers such as `Host` and cannot keep header order and duplicates, so neither can follow the forwarding rules (decision 7). A new connection per request avoids reusing a connection that holds an unread response, at the cost of a TCP (and TLS) handshake per request; connection pooling is left to a later version (decision 8). Letting the backend close first keeps TIME_WAIT sockets off the proxy host, whose ephemeral ports could otherwise run out; the proxy documentation states that risk. Express users get pooling from Node's `http.Agent` under `http-proxy-middleware`, which this first version does not offer.
records.implementationNotes: - Write the request line `METHOD target HTTP/1.1` and the header block in the layout of FR-PROXY-003 through a buffered stream over the socket, flushing before the body copy (FR-PROXY-007). Waiting for the backend's EOF after the response end is optional; if the implementation does it, the wait must be short and must not hold back the client's bytes or the slot release of AC-4. The TIME_WAIT and ephemeral-port warning belongs to the proxy documentation.

[D-376; r3 W2-005]

A finished scan produces the status `completed` with a findings table (dependency, identifier, CVSS score, severity), or the sentence `no findings`, and the report names the scanner version and the data timestamp. [D-376] Malformed CSV quoting and structurally incomplete data rows shall not be interpreted as a completed zero-finding scan; unsupported or out-of-range numeric scores shall remain unscored rather than low risk.

`docs/release/vulnerability-scan.md` exists and holds the report of the release run (`pending` with the reason, or `completed`), and the T50 vulnerability line of `docs/release/test-results.md` is `manual-pending` when the report is `pending` and `verified` when it is `completed` on the release machine, which a docs test compares. [D-376; D-381]

The report's dependency list excludes `compileOnly` and test-scope artifacts (the Servlet API, JSpecify, JUnit, Jetty) and includes the TinyHttpd components. [D-376] Audited false-positive suppression is permitted only when an exact non-regex package URL including version and one exact CVE jointly match; the initial audited pair is pkg:maven/org.jetbrains.kotlin/kotlin-stdlib@2.2.0 with CVE-2026-53914. The Kotlin Gradle plugin, every other artifact/version and every other CVE remain detectable. Source tests validate the suppression XML and reject broad or extra selectors; primary advisory, artifact inspection and build-only risk are documented separately. Genuine findings, including unsuppressed TinyHTTPD findings, remain in the scanner output and release gate. The optional -PnvdDatafeedUrl property configures the scanner NVD mirror and is forwarded to the child scan, allowing reproducible runs without a user-home init script; the selected mirror and its data freshness are recorded.

`releaseScan` runs the scanner in a child Gradle invocation with `ignoreExitValue` and writes the `pending` report when that invocation exits non-zero or leaves no report file, which the report writer's test covers with a stub exit code. [D-376; r3 W2-005]

records.requirement: The release build shall run `./gradlew -Prelease releaseLicenses`, which resolves the license of every dependency on the `runtimeClasspath` of the published modules, fails when any has a GPL-family license (GPL, LGPL or AGPL) or none that can be determined, and writes `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.md` at the repository root listing each shipped dependency as `group:name:version` with its license name and URL, and a default-build test shall fail when that file does not list exactly those dependencies.
records.rationale: Covers D-378 and T50. Measured (2026-10-20): the root `LICENSE` and `/Users/beom/work/git/TinyHttpd/LICENSE` both open "BSD 3-Clause License"; Gson, `com.google.errorprone:error_prone_annotations:2.48.0` (Gson's transitive dependency), `kotlin-stdlib` and `org.jetbrains:annotations:13.0` are Apache-2.0 and `slf4j-api` 1.7.36 is MIT by their POMs; `javax.servlet-api` 3.1.0 (CDDL with GPLv2 classpath exception) is `compileOnly` and therefore provided by the container, not shipped; `build.gradle` already writes the resolved graphs to `build/reports/naruserve/dependency-graphs.txt` (`checkDependencyRules`). Decision: licenses come from the POMs through an artifact resolution query; the TinyHttpd components come from an override table in `gradle/release.gradle` with the source `TinyHttpd/LICENSE` (the included build has no POM); a component with no license information and no override fails the task; the file also lists the compile-only artifacts under "provided by the container or the build, not shipped" with their licenses so the CDDL/GPL entry is explicit. Pitfall: the `slf4j-api` 1.7.36 POM has no `<licenses>` element; its MIT license is declared in the parent POM, so the resolution walks the parent POM chain before it reports a missing license. Pitfall: a dependency whose POM states two licenses (dual license) passes when at least one is non-GPL and the file lists both. Rejected alternative: a name-based allowlist of group ids; a new transitive dependency would pass unseen.

records.title: Express 5 HTTP string-path compilation with isolated legacy WebSocket routing

acceptanceCriteria.text: Literal text, named parameters, named wildcards, optional brace groups, quoted names, escapes and parameters embedded in segments match the pinned corpus; duplicate names are accepted with the later participating capture winning, wildcards yield segment lists, and nonparticipating optionals are absent.

Unicode identifier names, empty/unterminated quoted names, dangling escapes, unbalanced groups, missing parameter/wildcard names, reserved Express4 regexp metacharacters and ambiguous adjacent tokens are validated with a registration error and useful source position.

Full matching consumes the requested raw pathname except the configured optional single trailing delimiter; prefix matching stops at a path-delimiter boundary and returns the actual matched prefix. Case and trailing options are explicit; repeated delimiters are not silently normalized.

Matching preserves percent sequences in captured raw segments; slash splitting of wildcard captures happens before a single later strict UTF8 decode, so percent-encoded slashes remain inside their captured segment. Static literals are not globally percent-decoded before matching.

Optional-alternative expansion and generated matcher safety follow the pinned upstream fixes; adversarial ambiguity/backtracking cases are bounded and tested in a process with a deadline. License and source provenance for ported code are retained.

The compiler uses Java8/API21-supported code and existing dependencies only, has no shared Matcher execution state across requests, and does not alter the legacy RoutePattern/Router/RouterPolicy contracts used by existing WebSocket and explicit strict routing.

The public HTTP routing registration integration uses this compiler after its dedicated tests pass; feature completion requires integration-level routing evidence rather than the helper's existence alone.

records.requirement: The system shall compile HTTP string paths according to the pinned path-to-regexp 8.4.2 grammar into engine-free full or prefix matchers over the raw pathname, returning ordered raw captures and a matched prefix without changing the existing legacy/WebSocket matcher contracts.

records.title: Java Pattern route inputs and ordered path alternatives

acceptanceCriteria.text: An ordered alternative array/list selects its first matching alternative, with only that alternative's captures; invalid/null alternatives fail registration atomically. String, Pattern and nested alternative representations have a defined Java/Kotlin surface.

Pattern syntax and explicit Java flags control regex matching; search matching uses an independent Matcher for each match, does not impose HTTP string-path case/trailing options, and returns the actual matched substring for mount bookkeeping.

Numeric capture keys and supported named-capture access are defined using Java8/API21-compatible code; absent/nonparticipating groups remain absent, participating values decode exactly once using shared HTTP percent decoding, and malformed captures enter HTTP400 error handling.

Sharing a compiled Pattern across routes or concurrent requests shares no Matcher execution state. ECMAScript g/y lastIndex, JavaScript-only syntax and engine capture-source quirks are not emulated; JNI/Rhino/QuickJS/new engine dependencies are not introduced.

Registration overload tests cover existing two-parameter route handlers, three-parameter middleware-style callbacks, method references and Java/Kotlin ambiguity/nullness. Existing APIs remain available and string paths keep the agreed Express5 grammar.

A source-plus-initial-flags compilation path preserves Java Pattern lexical metadata exactly. Because Pattern.flags() can lose original embedded COMMENTS/UNIX_LINES state, a precompiled Pattern with genuinely ambiguous named-capture metadata fails registration clearly and directs the caller to the source-plus-flags path instead of silently mislabeling captures; ordinary unambiguous precompiled patterns remain accepted. Explicit RegexPathPattern inputs are supported by common registration, with Java8/API21 tests for the ambiguity and precise alternative.

records.title: Mounted HTTP routers with local options and merged parameter scopes

acceptanceCriteria.text: A mounted router owns its ordered layers and local case-sensitive/strict/mergeParams options; an app can mount routers and use middleware at string, Java Pattern and ordered-alternative prefixes without copying the child's live registration stack.

Prefix matches stop at delimiter boundaries, strip the actual matched raw text from the child URL, accumulate baseUrl and preserve originalUrl/query. Empty/root mounts and repeated/trailing/encoded delimiters have explicit fixture coverage.

mergeParams defaults false; when true parent parameters merge with child captures under pinned overwrite/numeric-key rules. Sibling routers and repeated nested mounts do not leak child parameters or local options.

next.router exits only the current child and resumes the parent stack; next.route respects Route identity inside the child. Completion, error and asynchronous exits restore parent mount views according to the oracle.

Existing group() remains an extension with its documented callback/middleware semantics; introducing dynamic mounted routers does not remove group/service/WS APIs. Java8/API21 and Java/Kotlin compilation remain valid.

records.title: Router-local named parameter preprocessing and cache

acceptanceCriteria.text: Callbacks run in the pinned runtime's actual captured-key enumeration order (including canonical integer-key sorting before other names), before selected layer callbacks, and receive the current decoded scalar/list value and name through Java8/API21-compatible continuation. Nonparticipating optional names are not processed.

Repeated scalar-string matches of the same name/value in one router invocation reuse that router's cached preprocessing result, including mutations and error/route-skip state; scalar comparison is by value, wildcard/list comparison follows reference identity, so freshly captured wildcard arrays across layers rerun hooks even with equal contents. Values changing and later recurring are tested against the last-match rule.

Separate routers process the same name/value independently; child mergeParams values do not spuriously trigger a child hook for a parameter not declared by that layer, and router exits do not leak the cache.
Multiple hooks for one name preserve registration order; delayed continuation, thrown errors, explicit errors and route/router skips compose with the shared request execution cursor.
Invalid callback/name registrations fail before mutating the router, and mutations affect the same Request object seen by downstream handlers and after-next observers.

records.title: SSE stream start and event serialisation: 200 with event-stream headers, field order, line splitting, name and id checks, data-only events and Last-Event-ID

acceptanceCriteria.text: A handler calling `res.sse()` gives the client status `200` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream; charset=UTF-8` and `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform`, each header present exactly once, and after the call `res.isCommitted()` is `true` and the response state is `STREAMING`, over the in-memory adapter and over TinyHttpd (T24). [D-326] Decision: `res.sse()` replaces any app-set `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control`, removes `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`, and sets status `200` whatever status was set. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-9 SDS-AC-6] Decision: when `ex.eventStream` throws a `RuntimeException`, the client is removed from the registry, the state stays `NEW` and the exception is rethrown so that the error path commits a `503`; an `IOException` aborts the response and returns an ended client. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-9 SDS-AC-8]

`res.sse()` on a response that is already committed throws `IllegalStateException` and writes nothing, and a second `res.sse()` on the same response throws `IllegalStateException`. Decision: `res.sse()` follows the single-commit rule of FR-HTTP-016. [D-326]

`client.send("connected", "ready")` writes exactly the bytes `event: connected
data: ready

` to the client (T24). [D-328]

`client.send("m", "a
b
cd")` writes exactly `event: m
data: a
data: b
data: c
data: d

`, and `client.send("m", "a
")` writes exactly `event: m
data: a
data: 

` (T24). Decision: every data line, including an empty one, is written as `data: ` followed by the line. [D-329]

`client.send(SseEvent.event("progress").id("100").data("{"progress":50}").retry(3000))` writes exactly `event: progress
id: 100
retry: 3000
data: {"progress":50}

`, the same bytes result when `retry` and `id` are set before `data`, an unset `id` or `retry` writes no line, and an event whose data is `null` or never set writes the single line `data: ` (T24). Decision: the field order is `event`, `id`, `retry`, `data`, as `docs/api/sse.md` shows. [D-330]

`SseEvent.event(n)` and `.id(n)` with `n` containing CR, LF or `\u0000` throw `IllegalArgumentException`, `client.send("bad\nname", "x")` throws `IllegalArgumentException` and writes nothing, `retry(-1)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`, and `SseEvent.event(null)` throws `NullPointerException`. [D-331] Decision: `checkField` throws on the calling thread before anything is queued, and the `retry` message is `retry must not be negative: <n>`. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-9 SDS-AC-11]

`client.send("only data")` writes exactly `data: only data\n\n` with no `event:` line, which a browser-compatible parser in the test dispatches as a `message` event. Decision: the data-only send is `send(String data)`. [D-339]

A request carrying `Last-Event-ID: 42` reaches an SSE handler in which `req.lastEventId()` returns `"42"`, a request without the header gives `null`, and the replay loop of the `docs/api/sse.md` example sends only the stored events after id `42` before the handler returns (T24). [D-337]
`client.send("ko", "한글")` writes the data bytes as UTF-8 (`data: ` followed by the six bytes `ED 95 9C EA B8 80`). [D-326]

changeNotes.reason: add-requirement
Feasibility=high (score 91). Blockers: none. Run: 2026-10-19.naruserve.wave-7.v01

records.requirement: The system shall, on `res.sse()`, commit status `200` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream; charset=UTF-8` and `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform`, put the response in `STREAMING` and return an `SseClient`, serialise each event as its `event`, `id`, `retry` and `data` lines in that order followed by a blank line with the data split at CR, LF and CRLF into one `data:` line per line, reject event names and ids that contain CR, LF or NUL, and expose a reconnecting client's `Last-Event-ID` through `req.lastEventId()`.
records.rationale: Covers D-326, D-328, D-329, D-330, D-331, D-337 and the data-only send of D-339; test T24. Measured: `Request.java:47` declares `lastEventId()` (verified under FR-HTTP-011 AC-3), so D-337 needs only an end-to-end check inside an SSE handler; `Response` has no `sse` method (`Response.java:9`). The event-stream format follows the WHATWG HTML "Server-sent events" parsing rules: a line `data: x` and `data:x` parse the same, an empty data line contributes an empty line, and EventSource dispatches an event without `event:` as `message`. Decision: each data line, including an empty one, is written as `data: ` followed by the line, so the data `a` followed by LF becomes the lines `data: a` and `data: `, and EventSource rebuilds the same string; lines end with LF; the fields are written in the fixed order `event`, `id`, `retry`, `data` whatever the setter order. Pitfall: a name or id with LF would inject a forged field; D-331 rejects it before anything is queued. Pitfall: `res.sse()` after `res.send(...)` must not write a second status line; it throws `IllegalStateException` like the other writers on a committed response (FR-HTTP-016). Rejected alternative: escaping CR/LF in names instead of rejecting them; silent rewriting hides app bugs, reopen never in v1.

records.title: SSE outbound queue, drain loop and heartbeat: any-thread sends in call order, handler-thread writes before the drain starts and the overflow policy

acceptanceCriteria.text: After the handler returned, 8 threads each send 500 distinct events concurrently to one stream with a reading client; the client receives all 4000 events, every event's lines arrive contiguous with no line of another event between them, and the events of each thread arrive in that thread's call order (T25). [D-333; D-406]

A send made from a thread other than the handler's thread is queued and written to the socket by the drain loop on the thread the adapter chose, which a test asserts by recording the writing thread in the in-memory adapter and finding it different from the sending thread. [D-406]

With `heartbeatInterval` 1 s and nothing sent, the client receives `: ping

` within 1 s plus 500 ms after the last write and again after the next interval, and with an event sent every 300 ms no `: ping` arrives during 3 s (T25). Decision: the heartbeat is the comment line `: ping` written after one heartbeat interval with no write, default interval 15 s. [D-332] Decision: the drain waits on the client lock for the time left until `lastWrite + heartbeat` and then writes `: ping

` itself, flushing after each event and each ping; no timer thread exists. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-2]

With `sendQueueSize(1024)`, a drain write held blocked by the in-memory adapter and sends of 100-byte events from a non-handler thread, the send that would make the queued bytes exceed 1024 returns `false` without throwing; once the write is released the client receives no event queued after the blocked one, the body ends, the `onClose` listeners run once, `isOpen()` is `false` and every later `send` returns `false`. Decision: overflow ends the stream (dropped event, discarded queue, ended body) and the overflowing `send` returns `false`. [D-406; D-339]

A handler that sends 600 events of 1 KiB each (more than 256 KiB in total) to a reading client before it returns, under the default `sendQueueSize` over TinyHttpd, delivers every event in order and leaves `isOpen()` `true` after the handler returned; the handler waits on a latch after its first send, and the test reads that first event from the client socket before releasing the latch, so handler-thread sends reach the socket while the handler is still running. Decision: a send on the handler's own thread before the drain starts is written, under the exchange lock, to the stream the adapter handed over through `StreamDrain.attach(out)` and flushed after the event. Deviation (recorded): D-406 says every `send` fills the outbound queue; until the drain loop starts, a send on the handler's own thread writes straight to the attached stream under the exchange lock, so the queue limit applies only to other threads' sends. [D-406; wave decision: Sends inside the SSE handler (r4 W2-001)] [committee decision: StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1)] Decision: that send takes `writeLock`, writes every queued entry in order and then its own event to the attached stream, flushes, and returns `true`; an `IOException` there ends the stream with cause `client` and returns `false`. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-4]

While the handler is still running, another thread queues events `A` and `B`, and then the handler thread sends `C`; the client receives `A`, `B`, `C` in that order, which a test asserts with a latch that holds the handler until `B` is queued. Deviation (recorded): until the drain starts, the handler thread writes the queued events and then its own event to the stream attached through `StreamDrain.attach(out)` under the exchange lock, instead of the drain loop writing every event. [residual: SSE send order before the drain starts (r5 W2-001)] [D-333] [committee decision: StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1)] Decision: when the drain starts it sets `draining` under the client lock and then takes `writeLock`, so a handler-thread write in progress finishes before the first drain write. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-5]

After the stream ended by client disconnect, `close()`, overflow or shutdown, `send` returns `false`, adds nothing to the queue and throws nothing, and the stream's queue holds zero bytes, which a test reads through the internal stream state. [D-406]

The test-fixture `InMemoryHttpAdapter` exchange's `eventStream` calls `drain.attach(out)` before it returns, with the same exchange-synchronized stream it later passes to `drain(out)`, which a test asserts by recording both instances; with a stub exchange whose `eventStream` never calls `attach`, a handler-thread send before the drain starts is queued under the `sendQueueSize` bound like another thread's send and the drain writes it in call order, which a test asserts. Decision: without an attached stream the core falls back to the bounded queue. [wave decision: Sends inside the SSE handler (r4 W2-001)] [committee decision: StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1)]

records.requirement: The system shall give each SSE stream a bounded outbound queue of `sendQueueSize` bytes that `SseClient.send` from any thread fills with whole serialised events, which the core drain loop of the event-stream extension point writes to the socket in call order, write a `: ping` comment after each heartbeat interval in which nothing was written, write a send made on the handler's own thread before the drain loop starts, after every event already queued, straight to the stream the adapter handed over through `StreamDrain.attach(out)` (falling back to the bounded queue when the adapter attached no stream), and end the stream when a queued send would make the queued bytes exceed `sendQueueSize`.
records.rationale:
Covers D-332, D-333, D-406 and D-339 (overflow policy), wave decision Sends inside the SSE handler (r4 W2-001) and residual SSE send order before the drain starts (r5 W2-001); test T25. Measured: `spi/StreamDrain.java` is the core-owned drain loop type of the D-106 event-stream point (IR-HTTP-007 AC-3), and `HttpExchange.eventStream(int, List, StreamDrain)` (`spi/HttpExchange.java:89`) lets the adapter choose the thread (FR-SSE-003: the TinyHttpd request worker). Deviation (recorded): D-406 says `SseClient.send` from any thread fills the outbound queue; until the drain loop starts, a send on the handler's own thread first writes every event already queued, in queue order, and then its own event straight to the committed stream under the exchange lock, so a replay loop inside the handler is paced by the socket and never trips the overflow policy, and the queue limit applies only to other threads' sends until then (r4 W2-001, r5 W2-001); `docs/api/sse.md` records it. Decision: overflow drops the event, discards the queued events, ends the stream and makes that `send` return `false` (no exception), so a broadcaster loop needs no `try`. Decision: queued bytes count the serialised UTF-8 bytes of each event. Decision: the heartbeat is the comment `: ping` followed by a blank line, written after one heartbeat interval with no write. Pitfall: a heartbeat timer that fires on a separate thread would need its own lock; the drain loop waits on the queue with the heartbeat interval as timeout and writes the comment itself. Rejected alternative: blocking the sender when the queue is full; it stalls app threads that broadcast to many clients, reopen on demand for a blocking `send` variant. Rejected alternative: queueing handler-thread sends before the drain starts; a handler replaying more than 256 KiB of missed events would overflow its own stream before the drain could run.
- [2026-10-20] Deviation (recorded), committee decision StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1): handler-thread sends before the drain (r4 W2-001, r5 W2-001) go to the stream each adapter hands over via the add-only `default` `StreamDrain.attach(OutputStream)` (IR-HTTP-007 AC-4), a second default method beyond W2-001's "one default method" wording. AC-5 now latches the handler so the test proves the write reaches the socket while it runs; AC-8 covers the in-memory attach and the queue fallback.

records.title: TinyHttpd event-stream class: chunked body on the request worker, NaruServe SSE counter with 503 before start, drain writes synchronized on the exchange

acceptanceCriteria.text: A class-reference test finds no call to TinyHttpd's `startEventStream` in `NaruServe-tinyhttpd`, and over a real socket an SSE response arrives with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, exactly one `Cache-Control` header with the value `no-cache, no-transform`, and an event with `retry` arrives as one block in the field order of FR-SSE-001. [D-335] Decision: the headers are written with `setStatus` and `setHeader` per pair, no `Content-Length`, and flushed once through `Body` before `attach`, so TinyHttpd frames the body chunked and the client sees the headers at once. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-11 SDS-AC-3]

The drain loop runs on the TinyHttpd request worker that ran the handler, after the handler returned: a test records the handler's thread and the thread of a drain write and finds them equal, and finds the drain write starting only after the handler returned. Decision: `eventStream` commits the headers and registers the drain, and `TinyHttpdExchange.run` runs it on the same worker until the core reports the stream ended. [D-335; wave decision: TinyHttpd feature hooks (W2-003)] Decision: a `RuntimeException` from the drain aborts the exchange. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-11 SDS-AC-5]

With `maxWorkers(2)` and `maxSseStreams(3)`, three open SSE streams and two concurrent plain `GET` requests whose handlers each wait 200 ms are all answered while the three streams stay open, so open streams hold one worker each and never take the HTTP worker share. [D-336]

With `maxSseStreams(2)` over TinyHttpd and two open streams, a third request whose handler calls `res.sse()` receives `503` with the standard error body and its request id, because the NaruServe counter throws a `503` `HttpException` before the exchange is marked started and the dispatcher's error path commits it; after one stream ends, a new `res.sse()` is accepted. Decision: `res.sse()` propagates that `HttpException` to the handler. [D-336; wave decision: SSE limit answer (r3 W2-001)]

`TinyHttpdAdapter` still sets TinyHttpd's `maxEventStreams` to `maxSseStreams`, which the existing limit-mapping test asserts, and no NaruServe code opens a TinyHttpd event stream, so the NaruServe counter is the only bound that answers `503` for SSE. [wave decision: maxEventStreams (W2-009)] [D-336]

`eventStream` holds the exchange lock only to check abort and mark the response started: on an aborted exchange it throws without writing a status line, and after it a `commit` or a second `eventStream` throws `IllegalStateException`; every drain write and every handler-thread write before the drain starts runs inside `synchronized (exchange)`, so a test that calls `abort()` while another thread sends sees the client stream end after a whole event and never receives bytes written after the abort. `eventStream` calls `drain.attach(out)` before it returns, with the same exchange-synchronized stream it later passes to `drain(out)`, and a test asserts both calls receive the same instance. [wave decision: TinyHttpd feature hooks (W2-003)] [carried: wave 5 drain synchronization (w5-P2-002)] [wave decision: Sends inside the SSE handler (r4 W2-001)] [committee decision: StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1)] Decision: inside one `synchronized (ex)` block `start` calls `requireStartable`, then `tryAcquire`, then marks the response started; the header set, the flush, `attach` and `register` run after the lock is released. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-11 SDS-AC-1]

When the client closes its socket, a later write or heartbeat of the drain loop fails with an `IOException`, the stream, which had no earlier recorded end reason, ends with the FR-APP-019 line `cause=client`, and the worker returns to the pool within two heartbeat intervals plus 1 s (with `heartbeatInterval` 1 s: 3 s), because the first write after the peer closed may still succeed and only the next one fails, which a test with `heartbeatInterval` 1 s asserts by opening `maxSseStreams` new streams afterwards and reading the access log line. [D-336; D-335; D-338]

Because TinyHttpd buffers the response body output, the stream handed to `attach` and `drain` is flushed after each event and each `: ping` heartbeat the drain loop writes and after each handler-thread write before the drain starts: over a real socket with `heartbeatInterval` 1 s, a single small event sent from another thread after the handler returned reaches the client within 500 ms of the `send`, and with nothing sent a `: ping` reaches it within 1 s plus 500 ms, each without further writes behind it. Decision: the core drain loop calls `flush()` after each event and heartbeat, and the TinyHttpd stream passes the flush to the socket. [D-335; D-332] [committee decision: StreamDrain.attach (wave-7 feasibility B-1)]

records.requirement: The system shall implement `HttpExchange.eventStream` on the TinyHttpd adapter as a chunked streaming body written through TinyHttpd's `Response.setHeader`, `flushBuffer()` and `getOutputStream()` on the request's worker thread and never through `startEventStream()`, run the core drain loop on that worker after the handler returns until the core reports the stream ended, count each open stream against a NaruServe counter bounded by `maxSseStreams` that answers `503` before the exchange is marked started, and hold the exchange lock only to check abort and mark the response started while every drain and handler-thread write synchronizes on the exchange.
records.rationale: Covers D-335, D-336, wave decisions TinyHttpd feature hooks (W2-003, SSE part: `eventStream` commits the headers and registers the drain, `TinyHttpdExchange.run` runs that drain on the same worker after the handler returns, drain writes synchronize on the exchange), maxEventStreams (W2-009), SSE limit answer (r3 W2-001) and carried wave 5 drain synchronization (w5-P2-002, commit 387db8c). Measured: `tinyhttpd/TinyHttpdFeatures.java:51` `eventStream(Response, int, List, StreamDrain)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` naming wave 7; `TinyHttpdExchange.java:240` `eventStream` is `synchronized` and takes the commit bookkeeping; `TinyHttpdAdapter.java:105-116` maps `maxSseStreams` onto TinyHttpd's `maxEventStreams` and sizes the worker pool `maxWorkers + maxSseStreams` (defaults.md: 192), so one worker per stream never takes the `maxWorkers` share (FR-ENGINE-004). TinyHttpd's `startEventStream()` writes a fixed `Cache-Control: no-cache` and its own `retry` block, which cannot meet D-326 and D-330 (D-335). Pitfall: checking the counter after the exchange is marked started would leave the dispatcher unable to commit the `503` (r3 W2-001). Pitfall: a drain write outside `synchronized (exchange)` races the abort path of wave 5. Rejected alternative: a dedicated SSE writer thread pool; it would add threads beyond D-416's budget, reopen if a non-TinyHttpd adapter needs it.

records.title: SSE stream lifetime: open after the handler returns, onClose exactly once, explicit close, HEAD on an SSE route, req.service in SSE handlers and shutdown from onClose

acceptanceCriteria.text: After the SSE handler returned, an event sent 2 s later from another thread reaches the client and `isOpen()` is `true`, over TinyHttpd (T25). [D-327]

When the client closes its socket, the `onClose` listeners run exactly once within two heartbeat intervals plus 1 s (with `heartbeatInterval` 1 s: 3 s), `isOpen()` becomes `false`, a later `send` returns `false`, and the FR-APP-019 line of the stream carries `cause=client` (T25). [D-334; D-327; D-338] This includes Servlet asynchronous errors or timeouts before the adapter starts the drain.

`client.close()` called from another thread writes every event queued before it, ends the chunked body so the client reads end of stream after the last event, and runs the `onClose` listeners once; a second `close()` changes nothing and runs no listener again. Decision: `close()` ends the stream normally. [D-334; D-339] Decision: when the queue is empty and the client is ended, the drain returns from its loop, calls `res.sseEnded(null)`, removes the client from the registry and only then runs the listeners, so the body ends before `onClose` runs. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-8]

Two `onClose` listeners run once each in registration order; a listener that throws is logged at ERROR with the request id and the next listener still runs; a listener registered after the stream ended runs at once, once, on the registering thread before `onClose` returns. Decision: `onClose` on an ended client runs at once. [D-334]

A drain write that fails with `IOException` on a stream with no earlier recorded end reason ends the stream, runs the `onClose` listeners once, logs the FR-APP-019 line with `cause=client` and lets the worker return, with no exception reaching the adapter's caller, which an in-memory test asserts by failing the third write; a drain write that fails with a `RuntimeException` ends the stream the same way with `cause=error`; a drain write that fails with `IOException` after `close()` was called keeps `cause=app`, the first recorded end reason of FR-APP-019 AC-10. [D-334; D-338] Decision: when the response aborts before any drain started, `abort` ends the client with cause `error` and runs the listeners, and a later drain call returns at once. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-13]

A `HEAD` request to an SSE route receives `200` with the event-stream headers of FR-SSE-001 and no body, and the response completes; inside the handler `send` returns `false`, `isOpen()` is `false` and an `onClose` listener runs once at registration; with `maxSseStreams(1)` over TinyHttpd, three `HEAD` requests followed by a `GET` that opens a stream all succeed, so `HEAD` takes no SSE slot and holds no worker after the handler returns. [wave decision: HEAD on an SSE route (r3 W2-002)] [D-327; D-334] Decision: for `HEAD` the headers are committed bodyless through the `end()` path, `ex.eventStream` is never called and nothing is registered, and `sse()` returns an ended client while `sseClient()` stays `null`. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-10 SDS-AC-11]
`req.service(Clock.class)` inside an SSE handler returns the same instance that `onStart` registered, which a test asserts by identity (T41). [carried: D-142 SSE case]

Over the in-memory adapter and over TinyHttpd, an `onClose` listener that calls `app.shutdown(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` returns from that call within 500 ms, and the app reaches `TERMINATED` afterwards, because the thread that runs the drain loop enters the request mark (`AppLifecycle.enterRequest`) before the loop and leaves it after the `onClose` listeners it runs, also when that thread is the in-memory adapter's own worker. [residual: shutdown from an SSE onClose listener (r5 W2-004)] [D-334]

records.requirement: The system shall keep an SSE stream open after its handler returns until the client disconnects, the app calls `close()`, the stream overflows, an error ends it or shutdown runs, run its `onClose` listeners exactly once when it ends, answer `HEAD` on an SSE route with the event-stream headers, no body and a client that has already ended, give the SSE handler the services registered in `onStart`, and keep the request mark across the drain loop and the `onClose` listeners it runs.
records.rationale: Covers D-327, D-334, wave decision HEAD on an SSE route (r3 W2-002), carried D-142 SSE case (T41, from wave 4) and residual shutdown from an SSE onClose listener (r5 W2-004); test T25. Measured: `internal/AppLifecycle.java:110-115` provides `enterRequest()`/`exitRequest()`, which `internal/GatedExchangeHandler.java:46` calls around a dispatch; `docs/api/lifecycle.md` ("요청 핸들러 안에서 shutdown") promises that `shutdown` called during a request returns at once, so the mark must span the drain loop and its `onClose` listeners for that promise to hold when a listener calls `shutdown` (r5 W2-004). The mark is thread-local, and the in-memory adapter runs the drain on its own worker thread (IR-HTTP-007 AC-3), so the drain thread enters the mark itself (AC-8). FR-HTTP-017 keeps `HEAD` bodyless; for `HEAD` `res.sse()` takes no SSE slot and runs no drain, so no worker is held after the handler returns (r3 W2-002). Decision: an `onClose` registered on an ended client runs at once, once, on the calling thread (removes the `docs/api/sse.md` marker); listener exceptions are logged at ERROR with the request id and the other listeners still run. Decision: `close()` ends the stream normally: the drain writes queued events, ends the chunked body and runs `onClose`. Pitfall: a client disconnect is seen only on a write, and the first write after the peer closed may still succeed, so the heartbeat bounds detection to two intervals plus 1 s. Rejected alternative: a background reader thread per stream to detect disconnects at once; it doubles SSE threads against D-416, reopen never in v1.

records.title: Shutdown of SSE streams: before-wait participant appends the closing notice, marks streams ended and does not wait

acceptanceCriteria.text: The SSE closing participant is registered in the before-wait phase of the shutdown participants of FR-APP-011 and, when run, first sets the stream registry's closed flag under the registry lock and then takes its snapshot, so a stream registered before the flag is in the snapshot, which an in-memory test asserts by registering a stream from another thread blocked on the registry lock. [D-436; D-445] Decision: the SSE `closeAll` is registered in `BEFORE_WAIT` before the WebSocket `closeAll`, and `terminate` in `FORCE_CLOSE`, once per app. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-7-11 SDS-AC-13]

During shutdown, the client of an open stream with two events queued receives those two events, then exactly `event: shutdown
data: shutdown

`, then the end of the chunked body, and the stream's `onClose` listeners run once (T44). Decision: the closing notice is the `shutdown` event with data `shutdown`. [D-341; D-436]

A stream whose queued bytes are within 10 bytes of `sendQueueSize` still receives the closing notice and ends normally, without the overflow end of FR-SSE-002, because the notice is exempt from the queue limit. [D-436]

With 50 open streams, one of whose clients stopped reading so its drain write blocks, the participant returns within 200 ms, because it only appends the notice and marks each stream ended without waiting for any drain. [D-436]

A stream whose client stopped reading is force-closed by the adapter stop at the shutdown deadline: its client socket reaches end of stream or reset within the shutdown timeout plus the D-344 margin, its `onClose` listeners run once, and the FR-APP-019 line of the stream carries `cause=shutdown`, the end reason the closing participant recorded first, although its drain write then fails with an `IOException`. records.requirement: The system shall register a before-wait shutdown participant that sets the SSE stream registry's closed flag under its lock, then snapshots every open stream and, without waiting, appends to each stream's outbound queue the closing notice `event: shutdown` with `data: shutdown`, exempt from the queue limit, and marks the stream ended, so that its drain loop writes the queued events and the notice, ends the chunked body, runs the `onClose` listeners once and returns its worker.
records.rationale:
Covers D-341, D-436, D-343 (SSE part) and the SSE part of D-445 (flag before snapshot; the behaviour of `res.sse()` after the flag is FR-APP-020); tests T44 (SSE parts). Measured: `internal/ShutdownParticipants.java:19-26` defines the `BEFORE_WAIT` phase "After STOPPING began, before the adapter stop waits", and `internal/DefaultRestApp.java:617-619` runs it before `adapter.stop(left(deadline))` (FR-APP-011). TinyHttpd's stop closes only its own event streams and upgraded connections and otherwise waits for a D-335 stream until the deadline, so without this participant every open stream would hold `shutdown` to the timeout. Decision: the closing notice is `event: shutdown
data: shutdown

`, dispatched to EventSource listeners of `shutdown`, with non-empty data because EventSource drops events whose data is empty; it is exempt from `sendQueueSize`. Pitfall: waiting for the drains inside the participant would spend the D-344 budget twice; the participant returns at once and the adapter stop waits for the workers. Pitfall: a stream stalled on a full socket never finishes its drain; TinyHttpd aborts it at the deadline (D-343). Rejected alternative: closing sockets without a notice; the client could not tell shutdown from a network failure and would reconnect at once to a stopping server.

records.title: Static mount mapping, directory index, several mounts, routes first, global middleware and the trailing-slash redirect

acceptanceCriteria.text: With `app.staticFiles("/", root)`, `GET /` returns the bytes of `root/index.html` and `GET /assets/app.js` returns the bytes of `root/assets/app.js`, both `200`. [D-256; T27]
`GET /docs/` returns `root/docs/index.html`, and with `index("main.html")` it returns `root/docs/main.html` instead. [D-257; D-261; T27]

With the mounts `/` on `rootA` and `/static` on `rootB`, `GET /static/x.css` returns `rootB/x.css` and `GET /a.txt` returns `rootA/a.txt`; with `spaFallback(true)` on the `/` mount, `GET /static/x.css` with `Accept: text/html` still returns `rootB/x.css`, and `GET /static/missing.css` with `Accept: text/html` receives the SPA index of the `/` mount. Decision: mounts are consulted in registration order and a miss in one mount falls through to the next, as with several Express `static` middlewares; SPA fallback runs only after every mount missed the file lookup, and then the first registered mount with `spaFallback(true)` whose prefix matches the path serves its index. [D-258; D-265]
With an explicit `GET /index.html` route and a `/` mount whose root holds `index.html`, `GET /index.html` returns the route's body. [D-259; T27]

A global middleware registered through `app.use` that sets `X-Mw: 1` runs on `GET /assets/app.js` served from a mount, the response carries `X-Mw: 1`, a global middleware that ends the response itself prevents the file from being sent, and one access-log line is written for the static request. [D-407; T35]

`GET /docs?x=1` for the directory `root/docs` is answered `301` with `Location: /docs/?x=1`; `GET /my%20docs` is answered `301` with `Location: /my%20docs/` built from the raw encoded path; and `GET //assets` is answered `404`, so no `Location` starts with `//` (a T29 case). [wave decision: SPA fallback exclusions; D-267; T29] Decision: the `301` applies to `GET` and `HEAD` of a directory without a trailing `/`, with `Location` equal to the raw path plus `/` plus `?` and the raw query when a query is present.
