records.title: docs/api/proxy.md and its English mirror document Proxy, its options and errors with the http-proxy-middleware counterpart, Java and Kotlin examples, and every limit and warning the request asks to document

acceptanceCriteria.text: `docs/api/proxy.md` starts with the navigation line `[English](en/proxy.md) | [문서 목록](README.md)` and `docs/api/en/proxy.md` with `[한국어](../proxy.md) | [API index](README.md)`; both name the module `NaruServe-proxy` with artifact `com.snoworca.naruserve:naruserve-proxy` that depends on `NaruServe-api` only, the package `com.snoworca.naruserve.proxy`, and map `app.use(path, Proxy.to(url))` to Express `app.use(path, createProxyMiddleware({ target }))` of `http-proxy-middleware`.

The page documents that `Proxy` is a `Middleware` whose option methods each return a new immutable instance, and lists every option (`connectTimeout`, `writeTimeout`, `readTimeout`, `totalTimeout`, `retries`, `retryDelay`, `retryUnsafeMethods`, `stripPrefix`, `preserveHost`, `bodyLimit`, `maxConcurrent`, `requestHeader`, `removeRequestHeader`, `responseHeader`, `removeResponseHeader`, `rewriteLocation`, `sslSocketFactory`) with its parameter types, default, accepted range and the `IllegalArgumentException` or `NullPointerException` the call throws, and with the `http-proxy-middleware` option it corresponds to or a statement that it has none.

The page documents `ProxyException` as an `HttpException` subclass with `kind()` and the seven kinds with their statuses (`CONNECT_FAILED` 502, `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` 504, `WRITE_TIMEOUT` 504, `READ_TIMEOUT` 504, `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` 504, `INVALID_RESPONSE` 502, `CONCURRENCY_LIMIT` 503), its `null` message and its cause in `getCause()`, that the proxy's own 400, 405 and 501 answers are plain `HttpException`, and that a failure after the response started aborts the client connection and is logged to the app logger, with an `onError` example that answers JSON by `kind()`.

The page has a Java and a Kotlin example of the request's usage: one shared `Proxy` with a fixed `requestHeader` and longer read and total timeouts, the path that must not be retried mounted with the defaults before the general mount that uses `retries(2)`, and the statement that the proxy calls no `next()` after forwarding, so the mount registered first under a prefix handles the request; the Kotlin example calls `Proxy.to(url).readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` without a wrapper.

The page warns that address-based checks are not reliable behind the proxy: a backend that looks at the socket address sees every request coming from the proxy (`127.0.0.1` on the same host), one that looks at the leftmost `X-Forwarded-For` value can be fooled by a client value kept there in trust mode, so checks such as allowing only localhost are bypassed and must move to means other than the address (an admin key, a separate port not exposed outside); it also advises against the legacy `trustProxy(true)` with the proxy because clients can forge the address under it.

The page warns not to set representation metadata headers such as `Content-Type`, `Content-Encoding` and `ETag` before the proxy, because the public `Response` cannot remove a header and an app-set value the backend does not send stays on the relayed backend body, and states that the `Date` header and the reason phrase clients see come from the gateway's adapter rather than from the backend.

The page documents the four timeouts with their defaults (connect 10 s, write 60 s, read 60 s, total 5 min), that none can be unlimited, that the first one reached applies, that they give 504 before the response and an aborted client connection after it, that the 5-minute total also cuts long downloads so such mounts raise it, and the two cases the total timeout cannot release: name resolution before the socket exists, which follows the JDK resolver, and time blocked in I/O with the client (a slowly arriving request body, a client that reads the response slowly), which is left to the adapter.

The page documents that retries are off by default and what `retries(n)` and `retryUnsafeMethods(true)` retry, and warns that the safe methods are an HTTP semantics distinction: a GET endpoint with side effects may run twice under retries, so such a path gets its own proxy mounted with retries off.

The page documents the thread model: a proxied request holds one worker thread until it ends; a client disconnect while the proxy waits for the backend may be noticed only when the response starts, so the thread stays bound until the backend answers, the read timeout or the total timeout; slow backends can use up the worker pool (`maxWorkers`, default 64) and make non-proxy routes wait, more so with a longer read timeout; and since there is no `maxConcurrent` limit by default, `maxWorkers` and `totalTimeout` are what bound the threads a proxy holds.

The page documents `maxConcurrent(n)`: an object created by it and the objects derived from it share one counter, calling `maxConcurrent` again on a derived object starts a new counter, a `Proxy` created by another `Proxy.to` call never shares, mounts without a limit are not counted, the same object mounted in two apps counts both, and a request over the limit gets 503 (`CONCURRENCY_LIMIT`) at once without waiting; with the example `Proxy p = Proxy.to(url).maxConcurrent(16);` whose `p` and `p.retries(0)` mounted on two paths share the limit of 16.

The page documents that every backend request opens a new connection and sends `Connection: close` with no reuse, warns that at high throughput the TIME_WAIT sockets this leaves can exhaust the ephemeral ports of the proxy host and that the root remedy is a connection pool, which this version does not have, and states that the timeouts are enforced by one JVM-wide scheduler that the first proxy request creates lazily, that lives outside the app lifecycle, runs a daemon thread that ends after it has been idle (within 30 s without proxy requests) and needs no shutdown hook.

`docs/api/en/proxy.md` states the same facts as `docs/api/proxy.md` for every item of AC-1 to AC-11, every Java block of the two pages compiles in `DocsExamplesCompileTest` or sits on its skip list with a reason, and every Kotlin block has exactly one compiled and run marker that `KotlinDocsMarkersTest` accepts.

[D-225; D-212; D-167; wave decision: Thread wording; wave decision: The default bind address is IPv4 `127.0.0.1`]

`docs/api/defaults.md` lists header size 16 KiB (`431`, `maxHeaderSize`), request-line length 8190 bytes (`414`, `maxRequestLineLength`, renamed from URL length), the per-line header limit of `inputBufferBytes - 2` (8190 by default, `431`, unchanged by `maxHeaderSize`), header count 100, header timeout 10 s, body-read timeout 30 s, write timeout 30 s, minimum body rate 240 B/s (`408`), the connection limits (workers 64, SSE streams 128, connections 512, derived wait queue 320, upgraded connections 128, per address 256) and the maximum of every setting; it states that no setting accepts an unlimited value, drops the sentence that `431`/`414` are not final, and the markers on these rows and on the unlimited-value question are gone. [D-225; D-437; residual: Upper bounds on size settings; I-012]

`docs/api/defaults.md` states that the bind default is `127.0.0.1`, that `bindAddress("0.0.0.0")` always logs a security warning and the app must add authentication itself, names `app.trustProxy(true)` for `X-Forwarded-*`, lists the D-400 transport-level rejections (`400`, `408`, `414`, `417`, `431`, `501`, `505` and the socket-level `503`) as plain-text answers that bypass `onError`, the error JSON and the access log, records the `421` Host rejection with the standard error body, and states that the TinyHttpd adapter has no TLS listener in v1; the binding and proxy markers are gone. [D-213; D-400; D-418; D-433; wave decision: The LAN warning is unconditional]

`docs/api/request.md` names `app.trustProxy(true)` in its proxy paragraph without a marker, and `docs/api/express-migration.md` maps `app.set('trust proxy', ...)` to `app.trustProxy(true)` and names `bindAddress("0.0.0.0")` in its LAN sentence, both without markers. [D-225; D-080]

`docs/api/README.md`, `docs/api/app.md` and `docs/api/json.md` name the bootstrap module `com.snoworca.naruserve:NaruServe` and the Gson module `com.snoworca.naruserve:NaruServe-gson` exactly as CON-BUILD-002 and CON-BUILD-005 fixed them, which a docs test checks. [D-230]

A test parses the defaults of AC-2, the JSON size and depth rows of `docs/api/defaults.md` and compares them with the defaults of `ServerOptions`, `app.jsonLimit` and `GsonJsonCodec`, failing on any difference; the Java blocks that call `server`, `trustProxy` or `ServerOptions` are compiled by the root docs compile test of OPS-HTTP-004 with no skip entry naming them. [I-011; I-009]

The other (미확정) markers that these decisions settle are removed in the same change: the sentence of `docs/api/defaults.md` on socket read/write timeouts, header count, wait queue and SSE/WebSocket connection limits names `headerTimeout`, `bodyReadTimeout`, `writeTimeout`, `maxHeaderCount`, the derived queue, `maxSseStreams` and `maxUpgradedConnections`; `docs/api/sse.md` names `maxSseStreams` for the concurrent SSE connection limit; the `docs/api/websocket.md` limits row names `maxUpgradedConnections` for the connection count while idle timeout, ping interval and handshake timeout keep their wave 7 marker; and the trust-proxy and LAN-binding bullet leaves the undecided list of `docs/api/express-migration.md`. [D-225; D-404; I-008; I-013]

records.title: CORS guidance for cross-origin auth clients in docs/api

acceptanceCriteria.text: The docs/api auth page and its docs/api/en mirror list Authorization (Bearer and the key scheme), Content-Type, X-CSRF-Token and Naru-Device as allowedHeaders entries, each with the condition under which it is needed.
The page states that a cross-origin request carrying Naru-Device while allowedHeaders lacks it is blocked at preflight and never reaches the server.

The page states that other-site SPA origins receiving body delivery in BOTH mode belong in allowedOrigins only, that adding them to trustedOrigins switches them to cookie delivery even though SameSite=Strict cookies are not sent on cross-site requests, and that a custom-scheme origin such as Capacitor's capacitor://localhost can be listed in CorsOptions.allowedOrigins but not in trustedOrigins.
The page states that app.cors(...) is registered before auth.install(app).
The page shows the CORS configuration as a Java example and a Kotlin example next to the Express equivalent, following the docs/api conventions.

The page states that a BOTH-mode client checks the body of every token-issuing response: accessToken present -> body delivery (keep the tokens, send Bearer); only csrfToken present -> cookie delivery (send X-CSRF-Token); the same client may receive either shape depending on Origin and trustedOrigins, so it never assumes one.

records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R29 (h) edition 33 (adds Naru-Device, which 05 §7 omitted) and R28 (CORS before install); §6.4 row "R29 × CORS 헤더"; CLAUDE.md API documentation rule (Express mapping, Java and Kotlin examples).
records.research: - Decisive facts: a missing allowedHeaders entry fails silently at preflight - the server never sees the request, so no auth log helps. trustedOrigins controls cookie delivery (FR-FLOW-002 ②), allowedOrigins only lets the page read responses; mixing them up sends SameSite=Strict cookies that the browser will not return cross-site. Rejected: auto-registering CORS headers from auth (CORS stays the app's explicit config; install ordering is the AUTH scope's doctor check).

records.title: Wave 3 decisions recorded in docs/api and their markers removed

acceptanceCriteria.text: `docs/api/request.md` states that `rawPath()` returns the raw, undecoded path without the query string (available through `req.query(...)`), gives its Express counterpart as `req.path` before decoding (not `req.originalUrl`), and has no (미확정) marker on the `rawPath()` row. [D-109; wave decision: Remaining markers]

`docs/api/request.md` states that `req.attribute(name, type)` throws `ClassCastException` for a stored value of another type, without a marker, and that a value is removed by storing a typed `null` variable because a literal `null` resolves to the read overload. [D-109; wave decision: Remaining markers; wave decision: Null attribute values]

`docs/api/response.md` states that `send(byte[])` without a `Content-Type` uses `application/octet-stream` and that `stream(InputStream, contentType)` takes ownership and closes the stream on success, failure or abort, with an example that does not use try-with-resources, and the marker line on these two points is gone. [D-109; wave decision: stream() closing; wave decision: Remaining markers]

`docs/api/routing.md` documents `app.routerPolicy(RouterPolicy)` with `RouterPolicy.builder()` (`mergeSlashes`, `ignoreTrailingSlash`, `caseInsensitive`, `enableTrace`, `enableConnect`) as allowed only while the app is in `NEW` (before `listen()`), like every setting in `app.md` (in wave 3 the internal implementation rejects a call after the harness freeze with `IllegalStateException`, FR-HTTP-008), replaces the sentence of section '라우팅 규칙 (wave 2 결정)' saying the policy setting API name is not decided with a pointer to `app.routerPolicy(RouterPolicy)` so that no sentence calls that name undecided, and states that `req.method()` returns `HEAD` during automatic `HEAD`; its marker set is checked by OPS-ROUTE-002 AC-3. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers; wave decision: req.method() during automatic HEAD; wave-3 residual: marker test of wave 2]
`docs/api/app.md` lists `routerPolicy(RouterPolicy)` among the `RestApp` methods with a Java and a Kotlin example and adds no (미확정) marker for it. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers]

`docs/api/defaults.md` names `app.routerPolicy(...)` with `enableTrace`/`enableConnect` as the explicit `TRACE`/`CONNECT` policy, and that row has no (미확정) marker. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers]

records.title: Wave 3 decisions in docs/api with the later-wave markers kept (wave 5)

acceptanceCriteria.text: `docs/api/request.md` states that `rawPath()` returns the raw, undecoded path without the query string (available through `req.query(...)`), gives its Express counterpart as `req.path` before decoding (not `req.originalUrl`), and has no (미확정) marker on the `rawPath()` row. [D-109; wave decision: Remaining markers] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC1

`docs/api/request.md` states that `req.attribute(name, type)` throws `ClassCastException` for a stored value of another type, without a marker, and that a value is removed by storing a typed `null` variable because a literal `null` resolves to the read overload. [D-109; wave decision: Remaining markers; wave decision: Null attribute values] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC2

`docs/api/response.md` states that `send(byte[])` without a `Content-Type` uses `application/octet-stream` and that `stream(InputStream, contentType)` takes ownership and closes the stream on success, failure or abort, with an example that does not use try-with-resources, and the marker line on these two points is gone. [D-109; wave decision: stream() closing; wave decision: Remaining markers] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC3

`docs/api/routing.md` documents `app.routerPolicy(RouterPolicy)` with `RouterPolicy.builder()` (`mergeSlashes`, `ignoreTrailingSlash`, `caseInsensitive`, `enableTrace`, `enableConnect`) as allowed only while the app is in `NEW` (before `listen()`), like every setting in `app.md` (a call outside `NEW` is rejected with `IllegalStateException` by the state guard of FR-APP-002), has no sentence calling that name undecided, and states that `req.method()` returns `HEAD` during automatic `HEAD`; its marker set is checked by OPS-ROUTE-003 AC-3. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers; wave decision: req.method() during automatic HEAD; wave-3 residual: marker test of wave 2] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC4

`docs/api/app.md` lists `routerPolicy(RouterPolicy)` among the `RestApp` methods with a Java and a Kotlin example and adds no (미확정) marker for it. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC5

`docs/api/defaults.md` names `app.routerPolicy(...)` with `enableTrace`/`enableConnect` as the explicit `TRACE`/`CONNECT` policy, and that row has no (미확정) marker. [D-398; wave decision: Remaining markers] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC6

`docs/api/express-migration.md` does not map `req.originalUrl` to `req.rawPath()`: the `rawPath()` row names `req.path` before decoding as its Express counterpart without a marker, the kept `req.originalUrl` row points to `req.rawPath()` plus the query read through `req.query(...)` without a marker, and the file states once, without contradiction, that v1 has no raw or text body reader, with no raw/text bullet in the undecided list (section 'Express에 있지만 아직 정해지지 않은 기능'). [D-109; wave decision: Remaining markers; wave decision: Body ownership] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC7

[wave decision: Remaining markers; D-137; D-192; D-225] re_stated_from: OPS-HTTP-003#AC8 (kept-marker set changed by wave 5)

records.title: Pinned Express 5 differential corpus and Java Pattern boundary

acceptanceCriteria.text: Reference provenance records Express 5.1.0, router 2.2.0, path-to-regexp 8.4.2, Node version, source/package hashes and a reproducible generator command; two unchanged runs produce identical fixture bytes.

Fixtures record registration success/errors, request method/raw path, handler trace, parameters and layer path/baseUrl, status, essential headers/body and completion/error transitions. Comparisons reject unexplained differences and report the case and differing fields.
The ordinary Gradle tests replay committed fixtures without Node, network or new dependencies, using the existing JUnit/test fixture/JSON facilities.
Negative tests prove that changed status, headers, body, trace, parameter values/absence/list shape and stale reference metadata are detected rather than silently accepted.

Java Pattern syntax/flags/matching differences are explicitly classified before corpus generation; ECMAScript RegExp engine equivalence, JNI and new ECMAScript engines are excluded. The remainder of the common HTTP contract retains Express parity.
Each implemented routing feature adds its positive, boundary, malformed/error and relevant regression cases to the corpus; no ignored/expected-failure case is used as completed feature evidence.

The Java replay adapter explicitly documents narrow language-specific error counterparts: Java route-syntax exceptions correspond to TypeError, decode failures to URIError, and the scenario's deliberately thrown plain RuntimeException to Error. Only the framework's informational path-to-regexp help-URL suffix may be omitted from registration messages; reason, source/index, malformed raw value, status and all response/trace fields remain checked. Raw reference and Java error information is retained for diagnostics, and negative controls reject unexpected error families or changed meaningful message fields; no blanket error/body waiver is allowed.

Decision: the heap bound is 64 MiB. Decision: the app's threads are counted by name, as the threads whose names start with `naruserve-` plus `tinyhttpd-acceptor-<port>` and `tinyhttpd-watchdog`, and the test runs in an isolated test JVM fork that starts no other app, because TinyHttpd's `tinyhttpd-watchdog` name carries no port. records.rationale:
Covers D-346 (T26), D-416, D-347, wave decision Thread total (W2-006) and its round-2 reading (r2 W1-001). Frozen D-416 bounds the threads of one app to 451: 192 TinyHttpd request workers (64 HTTP plus 128 SSE), 128 WebSocket read threads kept by upgraded connections, 128 WebSocket sender threads, one NaruServe idle-timeout scheduler thread, and TinyHttpd's acceptor and watchdog threads. Deviation (recorded): the bounded total is 452, because the wave 5 non-daemon `naruserve-keeper` thread (FR-ENGINE-006; `tinyhttpd/KeeperThread.java:11-35`) runs from bind to stop; the T26 bound and `docs/api/defaults.md` use 452 (W2-006, r2 W1-001). The stack figure is unchanged: 449 request-path threads (192 + 128 + 128 + 1) request 256 KiB each = 112.25 MiB, while the acceptor, watchdog and keeper use the platform default stack and sit outside that budget. Measured: `ServerOptions.java:41-54` defaults `maxWorkers` 64, `maxSseStreams` 128, `maxUpgradedConnections` 128 (defaults.md rows), and `TinyHttpdAdapter.java:105-116` sizes the worker pool `maxWorkers + maxSseStreams`. Decision: the T26 heap bound is 64 MiB of used-heap growth after `System.gc()` with 120 open connections, which is far below 120 full 1 MiB send queues because queues allocate only what is queued and T26 queues one message per connection. Pitfall: counting every JVM thread would include the test's own client threads; the test counts the app's threads by name prefix and by the TinyHttpd thread group. D-347 cannot be automated on a JVM; its AC is a recorded manual follow-up. Rejected alternative: a fixed WebSocket sender pool of 16 threads; D-320 forbids it (20 stalled sessions).
- [2026-10-20] Correction: the 64 MiB heap bound is far below 120 full 1 MiB send queues because queues allocate only what is queued, and T26 queues one message per connection. records.title: HashCost calibration, fixed cost and rehash thresholds at 80 and 125 percent

acceptanceCriteria.text: With a measurement stub reporting a cost that yields 123,456 iterations for the target time, calibrate selects 120,000
When the measured device would yield fewer than 50,000 iterations, calibrate selects 50,000; when it would yield more than 600,000, calibrate selects 600,000

HashCost.fixed(n) uses n iterations without calibrating the iteration count, and new hashes carry n in the hash string; the single start-time timing of one hash at n iterations (SEC-TOKEN-009 AC-7) sets only T and never changes n
With a target of 100,000, needsRehash is true for stored 79,999 and 125,001 and false for stored 80,000, 100,000 and 125,000 (00 §6.3 R27, R38 edition 8 S-5)
doctor reports the measured hash cost of this device (iterations and time per hash) at startup

Under HashCost.calibrate(t), the login timing logic uses T = t (00 R38: T is the current calibration target time): with calibrate(250 ms), a measurement stub, a fast fake hasher (so the elapsed time stays below 312.5 ms on any machine) and an injected scheduler, a failed login is scheduled at 312.5 ms plus 0-50 ms jitter after the request started (1.25T, the floor SEC-TOKEN-009 AC-2 asserts for this fixture). Under HashCost.fixed(n), where nothing is calibrated, T is the duration of one hash at n iterations measured once at start; that floor is asserted by SEC-TOKEN-009 AC-7 (open question Q45, decided 2026-11-02)

calibrate(250 ms) and calibrate(500 ms) are accepted and give T = 250 ms and 500 ms; calibrate with a target outside 250-500 ms (for example 10 ms or 5 s) never yields a T outside 250-500 ms: build() either refuses it with AuthConfigException or clamps it into the range (which of the two is an open question). With no HashCost set, the calibration target T lies in 250-500 ms (exact default value is an open question) (00 R5)

records.title: Low-priority rehash queue outside the hash slot

acceptanceCriteria.text: A successful login of a PBKDF2 user whose stored iteration count is below 80 percent of the target performs exactly one PBKDF2 verify (at the stored count) inside its slot, and the response does not wait for the rehash (00 §6.4 R38 x rehash): with the rehash hasher blocked on a latch the test controls, the login's 200 arrives while the rehash is still pending. For a legacy-hash user (MD5, SHA or bcrypt) the in-slot work is the legacy verify plus one target-cost dummy PBKDF2 (SEC-TOKEN-009 AC-1, 00 R38), and the rehash likewise runs outside that slot and the response does not wait for it (same latch test)
With 100 entries queued, the 101st rehash request is dropped without blocking the login, and the same user's next successful login enqueues it again
Exactly one worker thread serves the queue, it is a daemon thread, and it hashes only while holding a slot from the shared pool, so concurrent hashes never exceed the slot count
The char[] password of a processed or dropped entry contains only zero characters afterwards
If the user's passwordHash, ver, enabled or roles changed between login and the queued rehash, the rehash write is skipped (rehash compare rule of R37) and no exception reaches the login caller

records.requirement: After a successful login that needs a rehash, the auth module shall release the hash slot and place the rehash on a low-priority queue of at most 100 entries served by a single daemon worker that hashes only after obtaining a free slot, dropping entries when the queue is full and wiping the queued plaintext char[] immediately after it is processed or dropped.
records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R38 (edition 7 Q-8: rehash outside the slot on a low-priority queue capped at 100, overflow dropped and retried at the next login, one daemon worker that takes a free slot; edition 8 S-12: plaintext held as char[] and wiped immediately after use); §6.4 R37 x admin disable (re-read enabled differs -> rehash skipped).
records.research:
- Decisive facts: keeping the rehash out of the slot means the login itself does exactly one verify, so login timing and slot accounting stay equal for every account type (R38).
- Ground truth: the compare-and-skip rule for rehash writes (passwordHash, ver, enabled, roles must match the re-read row; only rehash is silently skipped) is owned by IAM's default field-method algorithm (R37); this queue only calls it.
- Pitfall: holding plaintext as String would leave it in the heap; char[] wiped with Arrays.fill after use (S-12).
- The worker stops with the auth onStop hook (AUTH owns install hooks).
- [2026-10-30] Clarification (A/B iter9): "the login itself does exactly one verify" above means one PBKDF2 computation per attempt. A legacy-hash user's in-slot work is the legacy verify plus the target-cost dummy PBKDF2 (00 R38, SEC-TOKEN-009 AC-1), so a verify-call counter sees two calls on a legacy success; AC-1 counts one only for PBKDF2 users (00 §6.4 row R38 x rehash).
records.implementationNotes: - Internal queue in utils.auth (e.g. ArrayBlockingQueue capacity 100 with offer(), single daemon thread; names not final). Calls UserStore.updatePasswordHash (IAM) through the decorator-aware path. Uses REL-TOKEN-001 slots and FR-TOKEN-003 chain hasher; no java.time.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A fake-JDBC MySQL connection records, in order: the session lock-wait setting, the `INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE owner_user_id = owner_user_id` executed with autocommit on, `setAutoCommit(false)`, `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on `naru_api_key_owner`, a `SELECT COUNT(*)` without `FOR UPDATE`/`LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, the key `INSERT`, `commit()`; no `setTransactionIsolation` call that changes the level (MySQL keeps the connection's level, so no isolation restore is needed), no plain read between `setAutoCommit(false)` and the `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, and no `WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT` text.

A fake-JDBC PostgreSQL connection records `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in autocommit, then `setTransactionIsolation(TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED)` before the `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, then a plain count.
When the count equals the limit the fake connection records `rollback()`, no key `INSERT`, and the method returns false.

A fake connection that raises SQLState `40001`, and in separate runs `40P01` and `55P03` (PostgreSQL dialect), at step 3 on 4 consecutive attempts: the store rolls back each time, retries from step 1 three times with delays between 10 and 100 ms, then throws; auth answers 503.

A fake MySQL connection raising error code 1205 at step 3 makes the store call `rollback()` before retrying from step 1. Raising 1205 at step 1 (autocommit on) makes the store retry from step 1 after the random 10–100 ms delay without calling `rollback()`, because the failed autocommit statement is already undone and `Connection.rollback()` is not allowed in auto-commit mode (00 §6.4 "R47 × 잠금 대기 초과").
An existing prefix raises `ApiKeyPrefixCollisionException` (not a generic store error).

A `JdbcApiKeyStore` built for the MySQL dialect, and one built for the PostgreSQL dialect, each return true from `supportsAtomicLimitInsert()` (construction API not final; builder style of FR-IAM-010, `JdbcUserStore.builder(ds).dialect(..)`).

records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R47 (3) lock procedure (26th edition, 27th edition plain count and lock-wait, 28th edition timing), retry (26th–27th editions), ApiKeyStore JdbcApiKeyStore note, §12 verification limits (InnoDB read view, MySQL upsert); §6.4 rows "R47 × MySQL 첫 발급 경쟁", "PostgreSQL 스냅숏", "교착 재시도 초과", "MySQL 기본 격리", "재시도 범위", "두 소유자 첫 발급", "잠금 대기 초과".

- Decisive facts: the lock row is created in its own autocommit statement first, so two first issuances for a new owner both lock it in turn at step 3 without deadlock. 24th-edition defect: inserting the lock row and then `FOR UPDATE` in one transaction made two MySQL transactions hold shared locks on the duplicate row and deadlock while upgrading; on PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ the count read the first snapshot and missed a just-committed key, exceeding the limit. MySQL InnoDB creates its read view at the first consistent read, not at transaction start, and `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` is a locking read that does not create it, so the plain count after the lock sees the previous holder's committed key even under REPEATABLE READ; this needs no `WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT` and no plain read before step 3. The plain count takes no locks, so neighbouring owners' gap locks never overlap. MySQL isolation is not changed because InnoDB READ COMMITTED accepts writes only with `binlog_format` ROW or MIXED (26th edition reversed the 25th edition change). MySQL 1205 rolls back only the statement by default, so the store rolls back itself. The procedure creates no deadlock within or across owners; retries are a safety net. - [2026-10-30] "No plain read before step 3" applies inside the step-2 transaction only (00 R47 (3): the count must be the first consistent read after the lock). Reading the session settings for restoration (REL-APIKEY-006) before step 1, in autocommit, is allowed. MySQL keeps the connection's isolation level, so the MySQL path makes no setTransactionIsolation call that changes it and needs no isolation restore.

records.title: SINGLE_INSTANCE default field-method algorithm under a per-user lock

acceptanceCriteria.text: With a store implementing only the five required methods, setEnabled(id, false) calls findById, then update with a copy whose only change is enabled, then findById again; the resulting row keeps the passwordHash, roles and attributes it had before.

A test store whose update() silently does not apply the change makes setEnabled, bumpTokenVersion and setRoles call update exactly 4 times (first try plus 3 retries) and then throw an AuthUnavailableException whose code is security_write_conflict (IR-AUTH-003 AC-6). On the HTTP path through the auth routers (for example logout ?all=true and A4) the answer is 503 with body code security_write_conflict (FR-AUTH-006 AC-3; for A4 the A4 handler's own answer, FR-IAM-014 AC-6), and on that path auth emits exactly one audit event security_write_conflict to the builder's AuditSink (FR-AUTH-009 AC-2). A direct call of the store's default method outside auth (for example store.setEnabled in a unit test with no Auth) throws the same exception and emits no audit event, because the default holds no AuditSink.

Under SINGLE_INSTANCE, auth's login rehash path re-reads the row inside the per-user lock and calls updatePasswordHash(id, expectedOldHash, newHash) only when the re-read passwordHash, ver, enabled and roles all equal the login-time copy; when any of the four differs (for example an admin disabled the user during login, driven by a hasher hook in the login test), no write happens, ver is unchanged, the disable stays and no error is raised. The default updatePasswordHash itself compares only expectedOldHash: it returns true and leaves ver unchanged on a match, and returns false without writing or changing ver on a hash mismatch. Over a test store whose update() silently does not apply, the default updatePasswordHash raises no exception (no security_write_conflict, IR-AUTH-003 AC-6) and calls update at most once; the rehash is skipped silently (00 R37).

Two concurrent auth-originated writes to the same user on one node (an admin profile PATCH and a logout ?all=true) never leave ver lower than the value after the bump: the final row has the profile change and ver = old ver + 1.
A profile write through auth (attributes change) never writes passwordHash, ver, enabled or roles values older than the row read inside the lock.
docs/api states that two admins writing the same user concurrently is last-writer-wins (docs test).

Under SINGLE_INSTANCE, while auth holds the per-user lock of user u (the lock that its profile write and its ver++ path take), a call of the default bumpTokenVersion(u) on the same thread completes without blocking and re-acquires that same lock object; a lock-identity probe records one lock instance for u across the five default field methods and auth's user write paths (profile write, logout ?all=true, password change, A4 disable), and while auth holds that lock a default setEnabled(u, false) from another thread blocks until auth releases it (00 R37 '같은 락'; REL-APIKEY-003 AC-6 relies on this).

records.title: changePassword atomic hash swap with ver++, null-hash equality and race retry rules

acceptanceCriteria.text: changePassword on a user with passwordHash null and expectedOldHash null succeeds, stores newHash and ver becomes old ver + 1 (SSO or legacy users can receive a password through admin reset or recovery).

changePassword with expectedVer different from the stored ver returns false and changes nothing; on POST /auth/password, where expectedVer is the request token's ver, a re-read ver different from it answers 401 and issues no tokens, and a re-read user with enabled false also answers 401 without calling changePassword.

Self-service change racing a rehash: the first changePassword returns false (expectation mismatch), auth re-reads, the new hash verifies the request's current password, auth retries once with the new hash as expectation and succeeds.

Self-service change racing an admin reset: after the failed swap auth re-reads the user and checks the hash before the session; the re-read hash does not verify the current password, so auth answers 409 write_conflict without a second write even though the reset also raised ver; an admin reset whose changePassword returns false answers 409 with no retry.
After a successful changePassword, ver has increased by exactly 1 and the hash is the new one in the same re-read; no state exists where the hash changed but ver did not.
The response body containing a new token pair is produced only when changePassword returned true (a test store returning false yields no token pair in any response).

With a store implementing only the five required methods whose update() silently does not apply, the SINGLE_INSTANCE default changePassword calls update once (the 3-retry rule of REL-IAM-001 covers only setEnabled, bumpTokenVersion and setRoles), the re-read still shows the old hash and ver, and POST /auth/password answers 503 with body code security_write_conflict and no token pair; the default reports the unconfirmed write by throwing an AuthUnavailableException with code security_write_conflict (IR-AUTH-003 AC-6), which the auth router ErrorMiddleware renders with that code (FR-AUTH-006 AC-3), not by returning false, so the AC-3 retry does not run.

A4 {password, enabled:true} on a disabled user with a matching re-read ver stores the new hash, increments ver once and then enables the user (the A4 success status of IR-IAM-005 AC-5); the store-level changePassword has no enabled condition (the statement's predicate is ver and hash only, also for an app-provided store).

records.title: Proxy request lifetime: synchronous on the request thread, the slot and the watchdog start after every check, and the slot, the watchdog and the backend socket are released exactly once at the end of the request

metadata.Tags: 0.12.0, feasibility:high, request-b, proxy, reliability, thread-model, concurrency, watchdog

acceptanceCriteria.text: Over real TinyHttpd sockets, when the client disconnects while a response body is being relayed and the backend is still sending, the backend observes its connection closed, and on a mount with `.maxConcurrent(1)` the next request reaches the backend; when the backend has gone silent mid-body, the adapter cannot see the disconnect until something is written, so the slot and the backend socket are released at the latest when the read timeout or the total timeout ends the relay.

On a mount with `.maxConcurrent(2)`, after 20 sequential requests to a stopped backend each answered 502, 20 chunked requests over `.bodyLimit(1024)` each answered 413, and 20 read timeouts on an app whose `onError` answers a `ProxyException` with 200, a request sent after the backend is restored reaches the backend.

A unit test that drives the relayed stream shows that calling `close()` twice, calling `close()` after the `onAbort` notification, and notifying `onAbort` after `close()` each return the slot once, cancel the watchdog reservations once and close the backend socket.

When `onError` runs for a `ProxyException` or for a 413 thrown while the body was being forwarded, the package-private counter of a `.maxConcurrent(1)` mount is already back to 0 and the request's watchdog reservations are cancelled.

After 20 requests refused with 400, 405, 501, 413 before reading or 500 for a consumed body on a `.maxConcurrent(1)` mount, the counter is 0 and the watchdog has received no reservation for them, because those refusals happen before the slot is taken.

The proxy connects, writes the request and reads the response header block on the thread that called `Middleware.handle`, and `handle` returns only after the response was handed to `res.relay` or an exception leaves it, as a unit test recording the threads shows.

records.requirement: The system shall make the proxy run synchronously on the request thread, holding it while connecting, sending the request and reading the response header block; take the concurrency slot and start the total-timeout watchdog only after every check and `req.bodyStream(...)` have passed; and, exactly once per request, return the slot, cancel the watchdog's reservations and close the backend socket — when the response was handed to `res.relay`, at the first of the relayed stream's `close()` and the `res.onAbort` notification, and otherwise just before the middleware throws or returns.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-121, PRD-216; fills: PRD-216 / hole / for AC-1, the in-memory test adapter never reports an abort, so client-disconnect tests run over real TinyHttpd sockets (design D-069); AC-2 ← PRD-120, PRD-122, PRD-218; AC-3 ← PRD-120, PRD-121, PRD-171; AC-4 ← PRD-120, PRD-122; AC-5 ← PRD-119, PRD-120; AC-6 ← PRD-118, PRD-237. `Middleware` runs synchronously on the request thread, so the proxy holds one worker thread for the whole exchange, and the first version answers that with the total and concurrency limits rather than an asynchronous middleware contract (decision 9). `res.relay` copies the body after the middleware returns, like `res.stream`, and the framework closes the stream after success, failure or abort, so that `close()` and `onAbort` mark the end of a relayed request; every other path ends inside the middleware. A slot returned twice would let more requests through than the limit, and one never returned would block the mount for good.
records.implementationNotes: - Guard the release with one `AtomicBoolean` per request, shared by the relayed stream's `close()`, the `res.onAbort` listener (FR-HTTP-035) and the `finally` path of the middleware, so whichever comes first releases and the others do nothing. Register the `onAbort` listener before calling `res.relay`; a listener registered after an abort runs at once (FR-HTTP-035). The in-memory test adapter never reports an abort, so disconnect tests run over real TinyHttpd sockets (design D-069, FR-ENGINE-014). While waiting for the backend the adapter may not notice an idle client disconnect, so the worker thread stays held until the backend answers or a timeout fires; the proxy documentation states this limit.

records.title: Proxy watchdog scheduler: one JVM-wide scheduler created lazily by the first proxy request, a daemon thread without context class loader that ends when idle, cancelled reservations removed, and timeouts enforced by closing the plain socket

metadata.Tags: 0.12.0, feasibility:high, request-b, proxy, reliability, watchdog, threads

acceptanceCriteria.text: Loading the `Proxy` class, calling `Proxy.to(url)` with options and starting an app that mounts it create no scheduler and no watchdog thread until the first proxied request, as the package-private scheduler accessor and a thread listing show.
Proxies of two different apps in one JVM use the same scheduler instance, and while 20 proxied requests are in flight at most one watchdog thread exists.
The watchdog thread is a daemon thread and its context class loader is `null`.

After every proxied request has ended and no new one arrives, no watchdog thread remains within 30 seconds, and a request sent after that with `.totalTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` to a backend that never answers still gives 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` after about 1 second.

The first proxied request after an app has started prepares the watchdog without calling `ApplicationContext.own` or setting an app attribute, throws no `IllegalStateException`, and its response is relayed.

After 1000 proxied requests completed under the default 5-minute total timeout, the scheduler queue holds no reservation, because each request cancels its reservations at its end and cancelled reservations are removed from the queue.
When a write timeout or the total timeout fires on an https exchange, the watchdog calls `close()` on the plain socket and never on the `SSLSocket`, as a unit test with recording sockets shows.

Stopping one app neither shuts down nor waits for the scheduler, and a proxy of a second app still running in the same JVM still gets 504 with `kind()` `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` from `.totalTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`.

While one proxied request is blocked writing a body to a backend that never reads it, the total timeout of another request still fires about on time, because a firing deadline only closes a plain socket and never waits on the blocked writer.

records.requirement: The system shall enforce the write timeout and the total timeout through one JVM-wide scheduler inside the proxy module, created lazily by the first proxy request that needs it and registered with no app lifecycle, running at most one daemon thread at a time whose context class loader is `null`, letting that thread end when idle so that none remains within 30 seconds after the last reservation ends, removing cancelled reservations from its queue, and firing a deadline by recording its kind and closing the plain backend socket — never the `SSLSocket` — without blocking.
records.rationale: AC-1 ← PRD-172; AC-2 ← PRD-170, PRD-172; AC-3 ← PRD-173, PRD-175; AC-4 ← PRD-173, PRD-219, PRD-257 (design D-066); AC-5 ← PRD-172, PRD-219; AC-6 ← PRD-171, PRD-174; AC-7 ← PRD-169, PRD-170; AC-8 ← PRD-172, PRD-257 (design D-066); AC-9 ← PRD-169, PRD-170. `SO_TIMEOUT` bounds reads only, so a blocked write and the overall deadline need another thread that closes the socket. NaruServe 0.11.0 offers no public way to register an app-level resource during request handling — `ApplicationContext.own` refuses after start and `attribute` has no atomic put-if-absent — so the scheduler is JVM-wide and lazily created inside the module rather than widening request A (decision 18). A daemon thread with core-thread timeout and no context class loader leaves nothing behind after a redeploy once idle, with no shutdown hook. Closing the `SSLSocket` sends `close_notify` and could block behind a stuck writer, which would stall every proxy's timeouts on the one watchdog thread, so the plain socket is closed instead.
records.implementationNotes: - Use a `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor` with one core thread, a keep-alive below 30 seconds, `allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true)` and `setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true)` (both available on API 21), created through a lazy holder or a double-checked `volatile` field; its `ThreadFactory` makes daemon threads with a recognisable name and calls `setContextClassLoader(null)`. A reservation records `WRITE_TIMEOUT` or `TOTAL_TIMEOUT` in the request's state before closing the plain socket, so the failing I/O maps to that kind (FR-PROXY-017). The proxy documentation states that the scheduler lives outside the app lifecycle (design D-066).

records.title: API key presentation through the Authorization scheme only

acceptanceCriteria.text: On a protected path, `Authorization: ApiKey nk_…` is verified as an API key, `Authorization: Bearer eyJ…` is verified as a JWT, and `Authorization: Bearer nk_…` is verified as a JWT and gets 401 `invalid_token`.

With `.apiKeyScheme("ak")`, `Authorization: AK nk_…` is looked up as a key (case-insensitive scheme) and `Authorization: ApiKey nk_…` is treated as no credentials: 401 `unauthenticated` on a protected path, and the 401 `WWW-Authenticate` names both `Bearer` and `ak`.
With `.apiKeyScheme("ak")`, `Authorization: ak.nk_…` is read as scheme `ak.nk_…`, i.e. no credentials: 401 on a protected path.

In each of HEADER, COOKIE and BOTH mode, `GET /x?api_key=nk_…` or a cookie other than `naru_at` holding `nk_…`, with no other credential, on a protected path gets 401 `unauthenticated`; the query value and cookie are not looked up as a key.
In COOKIE or BOTH mode, `Authorization: ApiKey nk_…` together with a cookie access token on a protected path gets 400 `invalid_request`; on a public path the request proceeds anonymously with no 400.

In COOKIE or BOTH mode, `Authorization: ApiKey nk_…` plus a `naru_rt` refresh cookie on an ordinary protected path authenticates with the key (the refresh cookie is not counted as a second credential).
An `Authorization` value of the configured scheme followed by an `#auth-param`-shaped value (for example `ApiKey a=b`) is a malformed key: 401 `invalid_api_key`.

records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R47 (1) (22nd edition presentation change, 23rd edition key characters and refresh cookie, 24th edition token68 strictness, 27th edition public path); §6.4 rows "R47 × 키와 JWT 구분", "사용자 정의 스킴", "점 구분", "쿼리 문자열", "키와 refresh 쿠키".
records.research: - Decisive facts: the RFC 9110 §11.4 grammar `credentials = auth-scheme [ 1*SP ( token68 / #auth-param ) ]` is used; scheme compare is case-insensitive per RFC 9110 §11.1. The `nk_` prefix is kept only so secret scanners find leaked keys; it is not used to tell keys from JWTs, so `Bearer nk_…` is a bad JWT. Query and cookie keys are not read because they leak into logs. Keys are accepted by header whatever `transport` is configured, so no CSRF token applies to keys. Key plus cookie access token is a multi-path credential (400, R30). The refresh cookie `naru_rt` is not an access credential, so it does not trigger the multi-credential 400. WebSocket Upgrade uses the same header and scheme rules (R40). Pitfall: telling keys from JWTs by the `nk_` prefix would let a client switch verification path by value shape.
records.implementationNotes: - Credential extraction lives in the auth authenticator chain (`spi.Authenticator`, scope AUTH/FLOW). Use `Request.headers("Authorization")` to see every header value. records.title: API key verification order on protected paths

acceptanceCriteria.text: An unknown prefix, a known prefix with a wrong secret and an expired key each get the same 401 with body `code` `invalid_api_key`.
A wrong key on `POST /auth/refresh` gets 401 `invalid_api_key`; a valid key on the same request gets 403 `api_key_not_allowed` (endpoint restriction runs after key authentication).
A stored key with prefix `aBcd1234` and a request prefix `AbCD1234`, with a store that returns the `aBcd1234` row for the lookup, gets 401 `invalid_api_key` (byte-wise prefix re-compare).
The owner is not read from the store or principal cache when the secret does not match (a store spy records no owner read for a wrong-secret request).

A store exception thrown by `findByPrefix` on a protected path gets 503 with body `code` `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`, not 401; the same exception on a public path lets the request proceed anonymously, and the error log is limited to once per minute process-wide.

A store exception while re-reading the owner in step 8 (ownerVer above the cached ver) on a protected path gets 503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`; the same exception on a public path lets the request proceed anonymously, and the error log is limited to once per minute process-wide.

Opt-in off or on: a key with scope `*` calling `GET /auth/admin/users` gets 403 `insufficient_scope`.
A `*` key issued without the opt-in, app restarted with `.allowAdminScopesOnApiKeys(true)`, the same key on `GET /auth/admin/users` gets 403 `insufficient_scope`.

A key issued with `auth-users:write` under the opt-in, app restarted without it: the key gets 403 `insufficient_scope` on admin endpoints, its other scopes keep working, and the key row is not deleted.
Opt-in on, key holding named `auth-*` scopes: granting the built-in `admin` role (`*`), disabling a `*` holder, or adding a user to a group that grants `*` each gets 403 `insufficient_scope`.
An admin holding only `auth-apikeys:write` issuing a key with scope `*` gets 403 `insufficient_scope` (new key scopes must be covered by the actor's scopes).

Opt-in on, a key with scopes `*` and `auth-users:write` whose owner holds `*`: granting user X a role whose scopes include `auth-apikeys:read` gets 403 `insufficient_scope` and X's roles are unchanged, because in the R31 (1) grant check the key's `*` does not cover `auth-apikeys:read` (00 R47 (5)).

records.requirement: The auth module shall reject `auth-*` scopes in key issuance unless `.allowAdminScopesOnApiKeys(true)` is set (400 `BAD_REQUEST` on PAT and admin issue, `IllegalArgumentException` in the app API), shall ignore stored `auth-*` key scopes in authorization while the opt-in is off, shall never let a key scope `*` cover an `auth-*` resource whatever the opt-in, and shall let no key scope cover a required scope `*`.
records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R47 (5) admin-scope opt-in (23rd edition), key `*` (25th edition removed the 24th edition opt-in condition), required `*` (26th edition), opt-off leftover keys (24th edition), R31 (1)(4); §6.4 rows "R47 × 관리 스코프 키 발급", "`*` 키와 관리 엔드포인트", "옵트인 켠 뒤 `*` 키", "옵트인 끈 뒤 남은 키", "R31 × API 키".
records.research: - Decisive facts: key admin power comes only from explicitly named `auth-*` scopes, which can be issued only under the opt-in. The 24th edition blocked `*` only while the opt-in was off, so enabling the opt-in instantly gave existing `*` keys admin power; the 25th edition made `*` never cover `auth-*` for keys. A required scope `*` itself is covered by no key scope (R31 (4)), so keys cannot grant `admin`, act on `*` holders, or add people to `*` groups (exception kept by 00: deleting an empty `*` group is not blocked by this rule). Residual risk under the opt-in: a key can grant roles to an accomplice or reactivate other disabled accounts within R31, and those effects survive key deletion; recovery is through the key id in audit events (doctor WARN at start, Javadoc on `.allowAdminScopesOnApiKeys`).
records.implementationNotes: - Apply the key-specific cover filter inside the R31 grant check (scope IAM owns R31; this requirement adds the key-actor rules). The opt-in-off ignore happens when computing the key's effective scopes. Doctor warnings are in the API key doctor requirement.

records.title: Common issuance rules: ownerVer source, owner lock and prefix-collision retry

acceptanceCriteria.text: Node B's principal cache holds ver 5 while the store holds ver 6; a PAT issued on node B gets ownerVer 6 and authenticates on its first use.

With the off-request stale-key deletion held (an injected executor that does not run queued tasks, so `deleteStaleByOwner` has not run; REL-APIKEY-002): a PAT issuance whose password check read ver 5, followed by `?all=true` on another node before the insert, produces a key with ownerVer 5 that gets 401 `invalid_api_key` and is listed as `stale`.
A store that throws `ApiKeyPrefixCollisionException` on the first attempt and accepts the second: issuance succeeds with a different prefix than the first attempt.
A store that throws `ApiKeyPrefixCollisionException` on the first attempt and on all 3 retries: the endpoint answers 503 `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` and the app API throws `AuthUnavailableException`.
Two concurrent issuances for one owner with 19 live keys through one `Auth` instance over a non-atomic store: exactly one succeeds and the other gets 409 `api_key_limit`.

`SINGLE_INSTANCE`, one `Auth` instance, off-request stale-key deletion held as in AC-2 (REL-APIKEY-002): (a) a PAT issuance is paused by a test `PasswordHasher` hook after its password check read the owner row at ver 5; the owner's `POST /auth/logout?all=true` then completes (ver 6); the issuance resumes: inside the owner lock it calls `deleteFutureByOwner(owner, 6)`, the stored key has ownerVer 5, a request with it gets 401 `invalid_api_key`, and it is listed as `stale`; (b) an admin issuance for owner S is paused after its R31 re-read read S enabled at ver 5; A4 then disables S (ver 6); the issuance resumes and stores the key with ownerVer 5; after A4 re-enables S (which does not raise ver, 00 R37), a request with that key gets 401 `invalid_api_key`.

records.requirement: Every issuance path (PAT, admin endpoint, app `issue`) shall set the new key's ownerVer from the owner row that the path's own check read from the store (admin issuance: the R31 re-read; PAT: the password check; app `issue`: the owner check), never from the principal cache and never from the `SINGLE_INSTANCE` in-lock re-read of REL-APIKEY-003, which only selects the `deleteFutureByOwner` argument (00 R47 (2) 27th edition, R47 (6) 26th edition), so a `ver++` between that read and the insert leaves the new key stale at once (fail closed); it shall call `insertIfUnderLimit` inside the in-node per-owner lock, and on `ApiKeyPrefixCollisionException` shall regenerate prefix and secret and retry up to 3 times before failing with `AuthUnavailableException` (503).
records.rationale: 00 §6.3 R47 (6) ownerVer source (26th edition), R47 (3) prefix collision and limit race (23rd edition), ApiKeyStore notes (per-owner lock, AuthUnavailableException); §6.4 rows "R47 × 발급 중 `ver++`", "prefix 충돌 반복".
records.research: - Decisive facts: the ownerVer source per path is the row read by R31 re-read (admin issue), by the password check (PAT) or by the owner check (app `issue`). Using the cached ver would make a fresh key stale at once when the cache is old. A concurrent `ver++` between read and insert makes the new key stale immediately: this fails closed, and the user re-issues. Counting and inserting separately would let concurrent issuances exceed the limit; the in-node lock makes a simple count-then-insert store safe on one node, while MULTI_INSTANCE needs an atomic store (doctor FAIL otherwise).
records.implementationNotes: - Shared issuance core used by `AuthApiKeys.issue`, the PAT handler and the admin handler. Under SINGLE_INSTANCE it runs the future-key deletion and pending-marker logic of REL-APIKEY-003/004 inside the same lock before inserting. Audit events for issue and revoke record issuedByUserId (scope AUTH events).

records.title: WebSocket connections opened with an API key

acceptanceCriteria.text: Upgrade with `Authorization: ApiKey <wrong key>` gets 401 `invalid_api_key` JSON and no 101.
Upgrade with a valid key expiring at T, wrapped in `auth.webSocket`: at `TimeSource` time T the session is closed with code 1008 and reason `api key expired`; a non-expiring key schedules no close.
Key deleted through another node's `DELETE /auth/me/apikeys/:id`: the connection on this node is closed at the next recheck, no later than `userCacheTtl` after the delete.
Key revoked through `auth.apiKeys().revoke` on this node: the connection opened with it is closed immediately.

Owner revocation through auth (00 R40 5th edition: a revocation auth causes closes on that node at once; R40 29th edition: connections on other nodes close at the next recheck, at most `userCacheTtl`; R47 (8): owner `ver++` and disable take effect at once on that node). The owner's `POST /auth/logout?all=true` through auth on node A (`ver++`, the key becomes stale): a connection opened with that key on node A is closed immediately, without waiting for the recheck; a connection opened with the same key on node B sharing the same stores is closed at B's next recheck, no later than `userCacheTtl` after the `ver++`. The same pair holds when an admin disables the owner through A4 on node A.
`SINGLE_INSTANCE`, marker (u, 5), connection opened with a key of ownerVer 6: closed at the next recheck.

Invariant violation at recheck: under `SINGLE_INSTANCE`, a file store whose `ver` went back from 6 to 5 after a connection was opened with a key of ownerVer 6 (opened while `ver` was 6): at the next recheck the connection is closed and `deleteById(keyId)` runs off the request path; under `MULTI_INSTANCE` on the MULTI_INSTANCE key fixture of OPS-APIKEY-001 AC-7 (the UserStore is a test fake that returns true from `supportsAtomicFieldWrites()`, so the app starts), node B's `UserStore` returns `ver` 5 while the key has ownerVer 6: the connection is closed at the next recheck and no delete call is made for that key.

Owner demotion without a `ver` change (00 R40 5th edition: the wrapper re-checks the principal every `userCacheTtl` and closes when it changed; R40 23rd edition and §6.4 row "R47 × WebSocket": the key row and the principal are both re-read at each recheck; R47 (8): owner demotion; SEC-IAM-003 AC-2: role and group changes leave `ver` unchanged). Fixed `TimeSource`, a connection opened through `auth.webSocket` with a key whose scopes are `posts:*`, by an owner that holds `posts:*` only through role `editor`: (a) role `editor` is removed directly in the store (`UserStore.setRoles`, not through auth), so `ver` is unchanged and the key is not stale: the connection is closed at the next recheck, no later than `userCacheTtl` after the change; (b) the same holds when the owner instead holds `posts:*` only through membership in a group to which `rolesOfGroups` (name not final) confers `editor`, and the test GroupStore stops returning that group from `groupsOfUser` (a change made outside auth); (c) a recheck at which neither the key row nor the owner principal has changed leaves the connection open.

records.title: Access log never records secrets and escapes control characters

acceptanceCriteria.text: A request `POST /login?token=qzv&password=pwz` with `Authorization: Bearer s3cr3t`, `Cookie: sid=c00k1e` and body `password=pwq2` whose handler answers `token-xyz` produces a line that contains none of `qzv`, `pwz`, `s3cr3t`, `c00k1e`, `pwq2`, `token-xyz` or `?`. [D-175; T39] Decision: the line is built only from the method token, the raw path without the query, the status, the duration and byte counts and the request id. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-4-8 SDS-AC-11]

A raw path containing `%0d%0a` is logged with the raw percent-encoded form, and an unrecognised method token or path containing a CR, LF, TAB, `0x01`, `0x7F` or `0x85` character is logged with `\r`, `\n`, `\t` and `\u0001`, `\u007f`, `\u0085`, and `\` as `\\`, so every access log record is one line. [D-176; T39] Decision: control characters U+0000–U+001F, U+007F and U+0080–U+009F are escaped this way. Decision: other escaped characters are written as `\u` plus four lowercase hex digits, and percent-encoded text stays raw. [SDS 2026-10-19.naruserve.naruserve-v1-wave-4-8 SDS-AC-12]
The access log line holds no header value at all. [D-175]

records.title: Each registration runs validate, watcher, apply, record in that order; a watcher exception vetoes it; post-start registration scope is unchanged

acceptanceCriteria.text: An invalid registration (a `null` handler, or a path the existing validator rejects) throws the same exception type as in 0.10.0, the watcher is not called, `registrations()` is unchanged and no layer is published (FR-APP-021 AC-3 still holds).

For a valid `app.get("/w", h)` made after `listen` with a watcher installed, the watcher is called on the registering thread before `get` returns; inside the watcher `registrations()` does not yet contain the `/w` record and a request to `/w` sent from inside the watcher through the in-memory adapter is answered `404`; after `get` returns, the record is present and `/w` is answered by `h`.

A watcher that throws `IllegalStateException` for `app.get("/w", h)` makes `get` throw that same exception instance; `registrations()` is unchanged and a request to `/w` is answered `404`. The same holds for `use`, `use(path, router)`, `param` and `use(ErrorMiddleware)`.

A registration the watcher accepted never fails afterwards for an input reason: for every kind, a test with a recording watcher that accepts everything sends a table of valid and invalid inputs; every invalid input throws before the watcher is called (the watcher never receives a record for it), and every record the watcher received is applied without `IllegalArgumentException` or `NullPointerException` from apply and then appears in `registrations()`.

After `listen`, `get`, `use(mw)`, `use("/p", mw)`, `use("/r", router)`, `param(...)` and `use(ErrorMiddleware)` are accepted, reach the watcher and are recorded; `cors`, `ws`, `staticFiles`, `group`, `onError` and `trustProxy` still throw `IllegalStateException` from the existing guard (`requireConfigurable`), the watcher is not called and nothing is recorded.
One Core test fixes the order: with a recording watcher and an instrumented app, the observed sequence for one valid registration is validate, watcher, apply, record.

records.requirement: The system shall process each registration as Core input validation, then a synchronous call of every registration watcher before the registration takes effect, then apply, then record, so that a watcher sees only valid registrations, a watcher exception leaves the registration neither applied nor recorded and reaches the caller unchanged, and registrations still accepted after start (routes, `use`, mounts, `param`) are reported to the watcher. Mounting a `Router` that already holds registrations is one registration whose watcher step covers the `ROUTER_MOUNT` record and every expanded record (FR-APP-026 AC-7). A `GROUP` registration is made only after its configurer returns normally and its apply step is empty: its inner routes are separate registrations that each run this cycle after the `GROUP` record (FR-APP-026 AC-2).
records.rationale: 00 §8 C4 contract (11th edition, order fixed in the 12th edition: "검증 → 감시자 → 적용 → 기록", one Core test) and R28 ("감시자 호출 시점", "기동 뒤 등록 범위", 11th edition), §6.4 row "R28 × 마운트 뒤 등록". If the watcher ran after apply, an out-of-scope route would already be live and `.protectOnly` would be bypassed; this makes the order a security property.
records.research:
- Decisive fact: `register` validates and applies inside one call, `http.methods(methods, path, callbacks)` at `DefaultRestApp.java:917` (L916 comment "Validate all inputs before publishing"), then records at L918; `HttpRouter.methods` (L54) is the same fused step. C4 must split validation out of apply and put the watcher between them (00 §8, R28 12th edition).
- Why validation first: so the watcher never sees an invalid registration, and a registration the watcher passed cannot then fail in apply for an input error (12th edition).
- Why apply before record: the record is the public truth; a watcher veto or an apply failure must leave the list unchanged so doctor and request-time checks (R30 14th edition) never see a phantom layer.
- Post-start scope (R28 11th edition, the 10th-edition "post-start CORS" rule deleted): only ROUTE, `use`, mounts and `param` are accepted after start; `cors`, `ws`, `staticFiles`, `group`, `onError` and `trustProxy` are already refused by `requireConfigurable` (`DefaultRestApp.java:824`, `AppLifecycle.java:62-66`). `use(ErrorMiddleware)` is still accepted after start (`DefaultRestApp.java:930` `requireHttpRegistration`, `HttpRoutes.java:15`), which is why `auth.errorMiddleware()` exists (R30 12th edition).
- Pitfall: the watcher runs inside the app's synchronized registration; a watcher that registers again re-enters. 00 is silent; open question (reject re-entrant registration or allow it).
- Pitfall: several watchers. 00 names one watcher per auth; whether a second watcher still runs after the first throws is an open question.
- Rejected alternative: calling the watcher after apply and rolling back on exception. A request served between apply and rollback reaches the unprotected route; reopen never (R28 final).
records.implementationNotes:
- Split validation from `http.methods(...)` in `DefaultRestApp.register` (L905-L920) and from the `HttpRouter` methods (L29-L66), so validation can run before the watcher for every registration entry point, including Router-originated ones (link from the mounted Router to its owning app).
- Keep FR-APP-021 AC-3 (atomic failure before publish) and AC-4 (post-listen registration with safe snapshots) green; the request in progress must still never see a partial registration.
- The ordering test belongs in `NaruServe-api/src/test/java/com/snoworca/naruserve/` beside the FR-APP-021 tests and uses `TestApp`/`InMemoryHttpAdapter` from testFixtures.

records.title: First-admin POST /auth/setup and recovery mode

acceptanceCriteria.text: With setup open, a local request (R33: loopback socket address, no X-Forwarded-* or Forwarded header) with the logged token, username and password creates the user and returns a success response; the same request from a non-local address is rejected and creates nothing, even with the correct token (in PROD a plaintext non-local request is 403 insecure_transport, SEC-FLOW-001 AC-6; a non-local request that passes the R33 transport check is the 403 setup_not_local of AC-8).

With setup open, a local setup body without a token field, or whose token is not a JSON string, is answered 400 BAD_REQUEST, thrown as a Core HttpException (00 R30 24판, §7 error-code row; IR-AUTH-003 AC-4), and creates nothing. A string token that does not match the logged setup token is answered 401 with code invalid_setup_token (IR-AUTH-003 AC-3; 00 gives no status or code, decided 2026-11-02) and creates nothing. After one successful setup, a second POST /auth/setup in the same process returns 404 NOT_FOUND.
When an admin (holder of *) exists and recovery is off, POST /auth/setup returns 404 NOT_FOUND.

With .recovery(true) or NARU_AUTH_RECOVERY=1, start logs a new one-time token and one WARN per start. Unless a null-password admin .user's account is missing (that case is AC-5: the body username must equal the .user name, else 400 username_mismatch, and the .user roles are granted instead of admin; 00 R31 (6), R41 11판/12판), recovery with an unknown username creates the user with admin, with an existing username enables it, replaces its password, grants admin and increments ver (old tokens rejected). After one successful recovery, a second POST /auth/setup in the same process returns 404 NOT_FOUND and changes nothing (user-state details owned by SEC-IAM-006).

Setup opened by .user("admin", null, "admin") with body username "root" returns 400 username_mismatch; .user("ops", null, "admin", "ops") setup creates ops with roles admin and ops. This holds although recovery is on, which a PROD setup opened by a missing null-password .user requires (FR-AUTH-004 AC-6; 00 §4.4, R31 (6)): PROD, .recovery(true), .user("admin", null, "admin") and an empty store, a local POST /auth/setup with the logged token and username "root" returns 400 username_mismatch and creates no user; with username "admin" it creates admin with the .user roles (admin), and no user root exists.
Recovery naming an existing service account returns 400 service_account_no_password and changes nothing.

Setup and recovery call no before event even when a beforeUserCreate listener always throws; they emit onUserCreated (or onUserUpdated for an existing user in recovery) with origin SETUP or RECOVERY, and each recovery use produces an audit event.

Locality is checked separately from R33 secure transport (00 §4.4 'local request and correct token'; §6.4 row 'R33 × setup'). PROD, setup open, correct logged token, username and password: (a) a secure non-local request (InMemoryHttpAdapter("10.0.0.5", true), req.isSecure() true) and (b) a request from socket 127.0.0.1 carrying X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7 and X-Forwarded-Proto: https with app.trustProxyHops(1) (req.isSecure() true) are each answered 403 with code setup_not_local and create no user; the setup token stays unused, so the same token from a local request (AC-1) afterwards still creates the user. 00 fixes neither status nor code; they were decided on 2026-11-02 (IR-AUTH-003 AC-3) and are recorded in docs/api.

records.title: Public path matching and optional authentication on public paths

acceptanceCriteria.text: With .permit("/health"): GET and HEAD /health without a token reach the handler; POST /health, GET /health/x, GET /HEALTH, GET /health/ and GET /%68ealth return 401 unauthenticated.
With .permit(Method.POST, "/hook") POST /hook is public; with .permitPrefix("/docs") GET /docs and GET /docs/a/b are public and GET /docsx is not.

On a secure transport a public request with a valid token has auth.userOrNull(req) non-null; with an expired or invalid token, or with two Authorization headers, or in BOTH transport with a valid Bearer plus a valid naru_at cookie (multiple credentials), the handler runs with userOrNull(req) == null and the response is 200, not 401 or 400. In HEADER transport a valid Bearer plus a naru_at cookie attaches the Bearer principal (the cookie is not read, R29 (g)).

On a plaintext non-local transport in PROD, GET /health without a token returns 200: a public path stays public on plaintext. The token-not-read behaviour on plaintext public paths is owned by SEC-FLOW-001 AC-5.

The credential endpoints are excluded from .permit matching: with .permit(Method.POST, "/auth/login") (and, in a separate app, .permit(Method.POST, "/auth/password")), a plaintext non-local POST to that endpoint in PROD still gets 403 insecure_transport and no credential is read (the login body is not parsed; the UserStore is not called). The endpoint list and the R33 transport check are owned by SEC-FLOW-001 AC-6.

A local plaintext request passes the R33 check (00 R29, R33 (b)). PROD, InMemoryHttpAdapter("127.0.0.1", false) (not secure), .permit("/health"): GET /health with a valid Bearer and no X-Forwarded-* or Forwarded header -> 200 with auth.userOrNull(req) non-null; the same request with X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7 added (not local, not secure) -> 200 with userOrNull(req) == null. In DEV (R41 turns the R33 check off), a plaintext non-local GET /health with a valid Bearer -> 200 with userOrNull(req) non-null. PROD with .allowInsecureTransport("TLS adapter pending") (R33 check off, 00 §6.4 row 'R33 × 아키타입 B'), InMemoryHttpAdapter("10.0.0.5", false), .permit("/health"): GET /health with a valid Bearer -> 200 with auth.userOrNull(req) non-null; the same app without .allowInsecureTransport -> 200 with userOrNull(req) == null (the plaintext public-path rule of SEC-FLOW-001 AC-5).

records.title: Principal cache with explicit invalidation and statelessAccess minimal principal

acceptanceCriteria.text: Within userCacheTtl a second request by the same user does not call UserStore.findById; after the TTL it does (fixed TimeSource).

An admin disabling a user through auth makes that user's next request on the same node 401 immediately (by default, and on guarded routes under .statelessAccess(true); unguarded routes under .statelessAccess(true) follow AC-7); a role or group change through auth clears the whole cache on that node so the next request sees new scopes; a change made directly in the store is visible within userCacheTtl.
A token whose ver is lower than the store's ver gets 401 (by default, and on guarded routes under .statelessAccess(true); unguarded routes under .statelessAccess(true) follow AC-7).

With .statelessAccess(true), on a route without a guard auth.user(req) returns a principal with getId() == token sub, getUsername() == "", empty roles, scopes and attributes, isLoaded() false and hasScope(any) false, and no store lookup happens.

With .statelessAccess(true), a route guarded by auth.require("posts:write") promotes through the cache, checks ver and enabled and decides on loaded scopes; doctor emits one WARN saying routes without guards see revocation only after the access TTL and that minimal principals should use only getId().

The grant rule (R31) is not decided from PrincipalCache: SEC-IAM-004 AC-4 owns the discriminating test (actor's scope removed directly in the store while the cache still holds it, next grant refused); this block adds no separate grant test, because a change made through auth already clears the cache (AC-2) and so cannot tell the two designs apart.

R44 exception: with .statelessAccess(true), after POST /auth/logout?all=true (one ver++) the old access token is still accepted on an unguarded route until its exp, but gets 401 on a route guarded by auth.require(...); the old refresh token, the old device token and an API key issued before the bump are rejected at once, and an open auth.webSocket-wrapped connection of that user on that node is closed (00 R44 5th edition K-15, §6.4 row "R36 × R44").

acceptanceCriteria.text: A log-capture test drives login, refresh, logout, a failed login, a protected request, an API key request, setup and a doctor run with known marker values for each listed secret (including a 40-character signing secret), once in HEADER mode and once in COOKIE mode, plus a BOTH-mode login whose response takes the cookie-delivery branch. records.title: Hop mode: after app.trustProxyHops(n), req.remoteAddress() is the nth X-Forwarded-For entry counted from the right

acceptanceCriteria.text: With peer `10.0.0.1`, `app.trustProxyHops(1)` and `X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.9, 203.0.113.7`, `req.remoteAddress()` is `203.0.113.7`; with `app.trustProxyHops(2)` it is `198.51.100.9`.

Spoofing is defeated: with `app.trustProxyHops(1)`, a client-supplied left entry in `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.7` gives `req.remoteAddress()` = `203.0.113.7`, whereas the same request under legacy `app.trustProxy(true)` gives `1.2.3.4` (FR-ENGINE-008 AC-2 unchanged).
Decision: several `X-Forwarded-For` header lines are combined in arrival order before counting, so lines `198.51.100.9` and `203.0.113.7` with `app.trustProxyHops(1)` give `203.0.113.7`.
With `app.trustProxyHops(1)` and no `X-Forwarded-For` header, `req.remoteAddress()` is the socket peer `10.0.0.1`.
The `Forwarded` header is not read in hop mode: `Forwarded: for=198.51.100.1` alone keeps `req.remoteAddress()` at the socket peer.

The in-memory adapter and the TinyHttpd adapter give identical `remoteAddress()` results for the same hop setting and headers, and no adapter class reads `X-Forwarded-*` itself (FR-ENGINE-008 AC-4 extended to hop mode).
